articles.title: Men's Rugby League World Cup 2026: Australia to face New Zealand in final as Samoa fume at decisions
articles.summary: Australia are one win away from a record-extending 13th men's Rugby League World Cup title after beating Samoa 44-12 in a fractious clash to secure a showdown with New Zealand in next weekend's Brisbane final.
articles.body:
Reece Walsh scores hat-trick as Kangaroos punish ill-discipline and errors from Samoa to run in eight tries and win 44-12 in Sydney; Samoa irritated by questionable refereeing decisions; Australia and New Zealand will also meet in the Women's Rugby League World Cup final next weekend

Australia are one win away from a record-extending 13th men's Rugby League World Cup title after beating Samoa 44-12 in a fractious clash to secure a showdown with New Zealand in next weekend's Brisbane final.

The Kangaroos, like their female counterparts , are pursuing a fourth consecutive title and if they do defeat their Antipodean rivals on November 15, they will earn a 10th World Cup triumph in their last 11 attempts, stretching back to 1975.

Sunday's second semi-final - New Zealand defeated Tonga 34-10 in the first semi on Saturday - was a repeat of the World Cup final in 2022 at Old Trafford in Manchester, which Australia won 30-10 to land a third title in succession.

In the rematch in Sydney four years later - preceded by Samoa's Siva Tau war dance in which Brian To'o put his forehead towards the face of Australia's former Samoa prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui - the away side were left fuming at some questionable refereeing calls.

Reece Walsh registered a hat-trick during Australia's eight-try victory as they pounced on errors and ill-discipline from Samoa.

Tom Dearden breached the Samoa defence for the converted try that put Australia 6-2 up in the eighth minute after the tourists had gone 2-0 to the good following a fifth-minute penalty.

Australia never trailed after that, with Jacob Preston, Tom Trbojevic, Walsh and Bradman Best also crossing before half-time to give their side a 26-2 lead - Walsh doing so after a Samoa try was chalked off for an alleged knock-on - and Spencer Leniu sin-binned for their opponents after remonstrating with referee Adam Gee.

Early in the second period, an error from Walsh allowed Stephen Crichton to score for Samoa, only for Walsh to atone with his second try of the game, profiting from a mistake by Ronald Volkman.

Samoa did not wilt and got on the scoreboard again when Izack Tago touched down in the left corner but when Walsh sealed his hat-trick to leave the score 38-12 just shy of the 70-minute mark, the game was all but done.

Samoa had a second try of the night ruled out due to contact between Francis Manuleleua and Liam Martin, a decision that once again left them fuming, before Australia extended their lead when Jack Bostock rushed in down the left.

Cameron Munster chipped in with six conversions for Australia, who rallied from an underwhelming group-stage campaign.

The only side to deny Australia the title since they lost to Great Britain in the 1972 final are New Zealand, with the Kiwis winning 34-20 in the 2008 final in Brisbane.

articles.title: Nations Championship - Ireland 42-12 Argentina: Hugo Keenan scores hat-trick in statement victory for Andy Farrell's charges in Dublin
articles.summary: Hugo Keenan notched a hat-trick as Ireland blew Argentina away in Dublin to secure a statement 42-12 Nations Championship victory.
articles.body:
Hugo Keenan (hat-trick), Dan Sheehan, Sam Prendergast, Ronan Kelleher score tries as Ireland secure dominant bonus-point success over Argentina in Nations Championship at Aviva Stadium in Dublin; Likes of Mack Hansen, Ryan Baird, Rob Baloucoune, Nick Timoney and Tadhg Beirne also shine

Hugo Keenan notched a hat-trick as Ireland blew Argentina away in Dublin to secure a statement 42-12 Nations Championship victory.

On a night of big positives for Andy Farrell's charges, they scored six tries through full-back Keenan's three, hooker Dan Sheehan, fly-half Sam Prendergast and replacement front row Ronan Kelleher.

Argentina scored two tries through wing Mateo Carreras, and actually landed the opener in the Test, but by 55 minutes the contest was over, with the visitors totally outplayed.

Ireland - Tries: Keenan (15,30,50), Sheehan (25), Prendergast (42), Kelleher (55). Cons: Prendergast (15,26,30,42,51), Frawley (56).

Argentina - Tries: M Carreras (10,46). Cons: Albornoz (46).

Indiscipline also proved a thorn for the Pumas again as centre Justo Piccardo and replacement lock Efraín Elias were shown costly yellow cards, with a vibrant Ireland needing little invitation to attack and score points.

A typically cagey and physical beginning to the fixture saw the visitors strike for the opening try in the 10th minute - wing Carreras claiming an inch-perfect Tomás Albornoz kick-pass over the head of final defender Craig Casey in a wonderful piece of playmaking skill.

The Irish response came within five minutes, though, as a Casey-led counter-ruck earned territory, before a scintillating backline move saw Robert Baloucoune arc round and make great yards at pace, Mack Hansen offload inside brilliantly, and Keenan collect to finish.

Prendergast added the conversion for an early lead after Albornoz had earlier failed off the tee, while three superb Irish turnovers soon earned them the chance to strike again.

First, flanker Nick Timoney exquisitely won a breakdown penalty by his own try-line to quell a Pumas surge. Then, Tadhg Beirne got up to steal an Argentina lineout, while Timoney came up with the breakdown goods again soon after - this time on the halfway line.

When Ireland kicked to touch and into 22, an intricate move off a lineout saw Sheehan play a blind inside ball for Timoney to charge forward. The Ulster flanker was stopped just short, but quick Casey service saw Sheehan fly over for a 14-5 lead.

Five minutes later, Ireland had their third try through Keenan again. Ryan Baird won another lineout steal to instigate the attack, with Ireland's full-back then doing marvellously well to battle and bounce his way over past a number of Argentina defenders.

When Prendergast converted, the Irish lead stood at 21-5, and worse looked likely to follow when Pumas centre Piccardo was sin-binned for giving away a cynical penalty in not being back 10 metres off a Sheehan quick-tap penalty.

Ireland failed to add a fourth score before the break, however, as Sheehan was illegally halted in the corner by replacement Leonel Oviedo - referee Luke Pearce just about decreeing penalty-only was sufficient.

Ireland put it behind them to score their bonus-point clinching fourth try less than two minutes into the second half, with Prendergast throwing a dummy bought by Marcos Kremer and racing in from deep.

The Pumas replied with their second try four minutes later, when centre Santiago Chocobares made the key break and Carreras powered his way over past Keenan, but Ireland then kicked on to another level.

The tireless Beirne won a trademark breakdown penalty deep in the Argentina half to earn the platform, with quick hands from Tadhg Furlong, Joe McCarthy and then Baird giving Keenan the space to dive over for his third.

With Baird continuing to cause havoc at the Argentina lineout with steals, the Pumas were soon back down to 14 players when the TMO showed images of Elias catching Keenan high in a shoulder-to-head tackle.

From the very next lineout, Ireland constructed a tight maul which drove forward at pace and was finished by Kelleher for their sixth try of the night.

Replacement Ciaran Frawley's conversion brought Ireland to their eventual 42-12 score, and head coach Farrell will be irked somewhat they failed to add more points from what was left in the Test.

Hansen showed some sensational skill and came close to both creating and scoring tries in what remained, but Kelleher's lineout performance was the central reason behind the home side failing to score more tries - the replacement coughing up a host of possession at the set-piece.

Farrell 'delighted' with win but warns: 'We have to be more ruthless'

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell said post-match:

"First and foremost, delighted to get the win and a good win at that. Six tries to two says a lot.

"Delighted to get the season off with a big win but I think the first game, we will learn a lot from that. It's a good place to be.

"We started really well in terms of being really clinical, we got into the 22 and scored two tries. We were dominant in that territory, which is what you want at this level.

"If you look at Hugo Keenan, Ryan Baird and Andrew Porter, lads who have not played international rugby in a while who have stepped up, Mack Hansen is another one, so I'm delighted for them.

"How we can be a bit more ruthless [is a lesson to take], because that's the team we want to be."

Keenan: Still a lot of work for us to do and get better at

Ireland's player of the match, Hugo Keenan said:

" You miss it. It's been 21 months since I've been here [Aviva Stadium] in green and it's been tough watching on.

"A bit like the rest of the lads, I'm just delighted to be out here and wanting to make this brilliant crowd proud and do them justice.

"I was at the end of three good plays, they were walk-ins to be honest, I'll take any.

"We got a bonus point playing against a really tough Argentina side. To beat them by 30 points and not play to our full potential is exciting because there is a lot to work on and get better at.

"We know every point counts. It's three tough games. We need to put ourselves in the best position and worry about what we can control."

"I think we were very good in patches, and some of the tries we scored were proper team tries.

"We'll be walking away from that game thinking we could have got a lot more out of it. There were some good parts for sure, but there's certainly a lot of parts we could have been better.

"It's a great starting point for us, we know we need to keep improving. Fiji will be a challenge, we know they like to throw the ball about, and South Africa after that, but all eyes on Fiji. We need to keep improving the performance."

For Ireland, they next face Fiji in their second Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin on Saturday, November 14 (8.10pm kick-off).

Ireland's Nations Championship fixtures and results

Argentina travel to face Italy in Genoa for their next Test, also on Saturday November 14 (11.40am kick-off GMT).

articles.title: Nations Championship - England 45-22 Australia: Henry Pollock stars out of position on the wing in morale-boosting Twickenham victory
articles.summary: Henry Pollock impressed out of position as Steve Borthwick's England claimed a much-needed, morale-boosting 45-22 victory over Australia in the Nations Championship at Allianz Stadium.
articles.body:
Jamie George, Ollie Chessum, Joe Heyes, Jack van Poortvliet, Henry Pollock (two) and Ben Spencer score as England ease pressure on Steve Borthwick with bonus-point win over Australia; Pollock played second half on the wing, replacing injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso

By Michael Cantillon at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham

Henry Pollock impressed out of position as Steve Borthwick's England claimed a much-needed, morale-boosting 45-22 victory over Australia in the Nations Championship at Allianz Stadium.

In a week when Borthwick came under intense scrutiny following newspaper reports of a summer rift with his England squad - claims denied by Jamie George to Sky Sports - England responded with a seven-try performance and record point haul against Australia.

Hooker George, back-row Ollie Chessum, tighthead Joe Heyes and scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet all crossed, while replacements Henry Pollock (twice) and Ben Spencer also got on the scoresheet.

Pollock, ordinarily a back-row forward, replaced the stricken Immanuel Feyi-Waboso (ankle) at half-time, featuring on the wing for 40 minutes and hardly looking out of place.

England - Tries: George (8), Chessum (26), Heyes (33), van Poortvliet (43), Pollock (55,57), Spencer (76). Cons: F Smith (27,34,43,58,77).

Australia - Tries: Jorgensen (40), Daugunu (62), Williams (74). Cons: Lonergan (41), Donaldson (75). Pens: Lonergan (12).

Fin Smith added five conversions and ran England's attack well from fly-half, while Australia scored via wings Max Jorgensen and Filipo Daugunu, and back-row Jeremy Williams, but struggled for parity in terms of the power stakes.

The Wallabies also suffered a costly blow when loosehead prop Angus Bell was sin-binned in the first half, becoming the first player penalised for a hip-drop tackle since World Rugby outlawed it this month.

England looked to have scored less than two minutes in when Feyi-Waboso scorched through, but the TMO soon showed replays of a forward pass from Ben Curry to Chessum earlier in the move to chalk off the score.

England kept up their early intensity, producing a choke-tackle maul turnover and attacking off the consequent midfield scrum with Feyi-Waboso central again, but that good work was undone by lock Alex Coles when he flew off his feet at a breakdown in the Wallabies' 22 to give away a penalty.

The hosts were soon back into the 22 when Australia coughed up a soft obstruction penalty under a high ball - Smith producing a fine kick into the corner - and from the subsequent maul, George was on hand to touch down.

Smith hit the post with the conversion, and soon Australia were onto the scoreboard via the boot of Ryan Lonergan, who split the uprights with a penalty after the England backline were caught offside off a lineout.

Superb work from Maro Itoje in the Australia 22 to charge down Lonergan then forced a knock-on, earning England a scrum to attack off within the Australia 22, but Heyes was penalised for an early push to see the chance blown.

Errors continued to flow from the hosts as Feyi-Waboso spilled possession on the run in the 22, George was pinged for crooked throw and a scrum penalty was shipped too.

Mistakes then proved contagious when Australia hooker Billy Pollard was pinged for a crooked throw himself in the England half, rendering the contest firmly top-start.

Feyi-Waboso soon displayed his pace and dynamism again at the end of a nice backline move, but England lost the ball again in the 22.

Yet, Australia just couldn't handle Feyi-Waboso and the pressure finally told as the wing made a burst down the opposite wing, and once England chipped the ball wide, Chessum was too powerful for Jorgensen to score.

Smith converted well for a 12-3 lead, before Itoje executed a strip for another chance - despite a couple of forward passes being missed - but a George Furbank neck-roll in the 22 saw the Wallabies clear.

Australia were then reduced to 14, however, as the TMO showed images of a Bell hip-drop tackle on Feyi-Waboso.

Henry Slade kicked to corner, and the maul did the trick again as Heyes wrestled the ball out and dived over for England's third of the half.

Two minutes before half-time, Tommy Freeman should have scored England's fourth but knocked on a bouncing ball in-goal after winning the chase.

Instead, the visitors notched a try out of nothing in the final minute before half-time; Jorgenson intercepting a telegraphed Van Poortvliet pass near halfway and showing his pace to sprint over.

That left the half-time deficit a nine-point one, but just before Bell was due to re-emerge from his sin-bin period, England scored their fourth three minutes into the second half: Pollock carrying brilliantly down the left to start things, and Freeman doing fabulous work down the right before finding Van Poorvliet with a long pass.

Australia threatened a try back in response when centre Isaac Henry cut through England and broke to near the 22, but the Wallabies were pinged for sealing off.

Henry then made a big error in skewing a kick out on the full as the Wallabies sought to attack from deep, and England did not let up until they had a fifth try as Pollock finished out wide after Australia had been pushed back in tight carries near the try-line.

Within two minutes, Pollock was celebrating again, as another rapid backline attack well-orchestrated by Smith saw the makeshift wing finish with swagger down the right.

Past the hour mark, the Wallabies did score again as Daugunu finished a flowing move in the left corner, but it went unconverted when Lonergan couldn't land the tough kick.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii passed up a certain try when he shipped the ball to Jorgensen instead of finishing, but Australia scored from the resulting England lineout in any case - the hosts sloppy near their own try-line and Williams finishing.

England soon forgot about that mistake, though, as Spencer intercepted a Daugunu offload to race into the corner and round off a big victory.

Pollock: Coaches wouldn't put me on wing if they didn't think I could do it

"The biggest thing is the rugby stuff. Pleasure and privilege. For me, the biggest thing is going out there and showcasing myself and the growth of this team throughout the summer and into the autumn.

"I love playing for this team, I love playing back at home. We spoke about being back at home and creating some energy around that.

"The coaches wouldn't put me on the wing if they knew I couldn't do anything there, so the big thing for me is going out there and being as confident as I can.

"If I mess up, I'm playing a new position, I'm going to make some new learnings from it. If there's any young kids out there, playing new positions, just take each step as it comes.

"I made a few mistakes today, but the boys outside me, like Slade in the corner, backed me up. That just made my job so much easier.

"I disagree with that [versatility potentially working agasint him], versatility is a massive thing. Today, my role was coming on in the second half and being a winger. I trust the coaches and the team, whatever they need to do for that.

"It showed in that last 30-40 minutes, the bench came on and did their thing. That shows where we're at as a squad."

George 'proud' of team-mates after tough week

"I wonder where that's come from? [big try celebration]

"It's [newspaper reports] been a distraction. I'm so unbelievably proud of how the team looked after each other, stepped up for each other, and we are a tight team regardless.

"As I said, it probably brought us even tighter and being back at Allianz Stadium is just unbelievable."

England captain Maro Itoje said to ITV Sport:

"I am over the moon. This week has been great, great for me personally to be back in camp.

"I think we're starting to show what we can do, we've got a very talented team, and it's now time for us to put it all together.

"Sometimes when you have time away from the team, as I did in the summer, it makes you appreciate what playing for England is all about.

"When I stood out there for the National Anthems, it gave me goosebumps. These are the games I want to be a part of."

Wilson: We can't be waiting until last 15 minutes to start playing

Australia captain Harry Wilson told ITV Sport:

"England put us under the pump, we didn't get too much ball in the first-half. We didn't get too many A-zone entries and England were the better team today.

"They fronted up physically, put us under the pump. Our defence wasn't physical enough in slowing the ball down.

"I feel like we were playing from behind there, so, credit to England.

"A lot of our issues might be mindset. We've got seven days to take some feedback from this game and make sure we're a lot better.

"I know Scotland are a really good team, and we have to be ready for it, and we have to be ready for these harsh lessons.

"We know when we hold the ball for long phases and play our style of footy, we can cut teams up. But we can't be waiting for the last 15 minutes to do it."

For England, they next face Japan in their second Nations Championship Test of the autumn at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Saturday November 14 (4.40pm kick-off).

England's Nations Championship fixtures and results

Australia travel to face Scotland at Murrayfield for their next Test, on Sunday November 15 (3.10pm kick-off).

articles.title: Nations Championship - Scotland 21-43 New Zealand: All Blacks power on to leave hosts well short of history at Murrayfield
articles.summary: Scotland remain winless against New Zealand in 121 years of contests as the All Blacks proved too strong to record a 43-21 Nations Championship victory at Murrayfield.
articles.body:
Wallace Sititi, Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor, Beauden Barrett (two), Josh Moorby, Asafo Aumua score as New Zealand's All Blacks surge on in second half to comprehensively beat Scotland at Murrayfield in Nations Championship; Scots fail to score four tries, meaning they earn no bonus point

Scotland remain winless against New Zealand in 121 years of contests as the All Blacks proved too strong to record a 43-21 Nations Championship victory at Murrayfield.

The All Blacks scored seven tries in the Scottish capital through No 8 Wallace Sititi, loosehead Ethan de Groot, hooker Codie Taylor, full-back Beauden Barrett (two), wing Josh Moorby and replacement hooker Asafo Aumua, and despite sin-binings to back-rows Peter Lakai and Sititi, demonstrated their lethal ability in attack.

Scotland battled from 10 points behind to narrow to within three by the break after a madcap opening 40 minutes which saw hooker Ewan Ashman score a hat-trick, but New Zealand emerged to dominate the second half.

Scotland 21-43 New Zealand - Score summary

Scotland - Tries: Ashman (8,26,38). Cons: Russell (9, 27, 39).

New Zealand - Tries: Sititi (4), de Groot (16), Lakai (20), B Barrett (31,51), Moorby (49), Aumua (68). Cons: McKenzie (17,32,52,69).

The net result means Gregor Townsend's side remain searching for a first success over the All Blacks, with Scotland's winless run against New Zealand now at 34 Tests.

With Scotland caught offside less than three minutes in, New Zealand turned down a potential kick for points in favour of a lineout attack in the 22, and struck for the opening try through a clever set-piece play filled with disguise as Sititi spun and raced over.

McKenzie poorly missed the conversion and within four minutes, Scotland had their first try: a rolling maul seeing the hosts plunge the majority of their outfield players in, rendering it unstoppable, with Ashman finishing.

Russell converted for an early lead, but the All Blacks replied with two bouts of sustained phase-attack in the Scotland 22: the first seeing Will Jordan held up, but the second bringing a try for De Groot as the prop grounded on the line.

McKenzie converted this time for a 12-7 lead, and it was soon extended further when Scotland No 8 Jack Dempsey gave away an extremely costly neck-roll penalty within his own 22 - the All Blacks making him pay with a rapid maul drive off a flat and sharp Taylor lineout delivery - the hooker adding the scoring touch.

McKenzie proved off target again with the conversion to leave the difference a 10-point one, and when the visitors conceded five penalties in quick succession to invite Scottish pressure in their 22, Lakai was sent to the sin-bin and Russell kicked back into the corner.

Incisive Scotland centre Huw Jones - outstanding in the first half - was held up in-goal when a try looked a certainty, but Scotland did notch their second in the 26th minute when Ashman ran a superb line to charge past Sititi to finish.

Russell tapped over the extras to narrow within three points, but the 14-player All Blacks were next to cross when Barrett sliced through following a trademark slick attack.

Scotland's response was to make another line-break off a restart, with the All Blacks guilty of yet more penalties and temporarily reduced to 13 with Sititi sin-binned.

Yet, in the home side's only attack facing 13 players, they saw a five-metre lineout maul sacked and the ball forced unplayable in a huge lost opportunity, which was then compounded when the All Blacks won a dominant scrum penalty to clear.

Another Jones break saw New Zealand infringe to present a five-metre lineout chance once more, and this time Scotland got it right two minutes before the break as backs piled into the maul again and Ashman completed his hat-trick.

Russell's conversion brought Scotland within three again by the half-time break, and an early chance fell their way in the second half on the cusp of the New Zealand 22 with ball in hand, but poor execution saw the ball fall to floor.

Instead, Scotland captain Tuipulotu was caught offside to invite New Zealand onto the attack, pinning the hosts into their 22. When a crooked lineout throw followed, New Zealand turned the screw at the scrum and scored out wide through Moorby.

The All Blacks quickly built into the 22 moments later, with Tuipulotu sin-binned for repeat team infringements and Barrett finishing his second in the 51st minute after ruthless New Zealand backline attack vs 14.

McKenzie converted for a substantial 15-point lead, which felt even greater when Scotland passed up their next try chance: wing Kyle Steyn knocking on after Jordan failed to get a hand to a long pass just in front of him.

Russell was subbed off for Scotland just past the hour having struggled to influence things, while breakdown penalties won by Jordie Barrett and Quinn Tupaea sniffed out the home side's next two possessions.

With 12 minutes to play, New Zealand chalked up their seventh try of the Test as Aumua sprinted through untouched past poor Scotland defence.

Searching for a fourth try which would at least have brought Scotland a bonus point in defeat, New Zealand's closing defence proved too good, leaving those in blue with a familiar deflating feeling.

For Scotland, they next face Australia in their second Nations Championship Test of the autumn at Murrayfield on Sunday November 15 (3.10pm kick-off).

Scotland's Nations Championship fixtures and results

New Zealand travel to face Wales in Cardiff for their next Test, on Saturday November 14 (2.10pm kick-off).

articles.title: Nations Championship: Wales opt for centre power pair against Japan
articles.summary: Wales head coach Steve Tandy has selected Max Llewellyn alongside Eddie James in midfield to face Japan in the Nations Championship on Saturday.
articles.body:
Wales head coach Steve Tandy has opted for power in his centre partnership by bringing in Max Llewellyn alongside Eddie James for the Nations Championship opener against Japan on Saturday (16:40 GMT).

Llewellyn, 6ft 6in (1.96m) and 16st 12lbs (107kg) and James, 6ft 4in (1.90m) and 16st 3lbs (103kg), will form one of Wales' biggest midfield combinations.

Tandy has abandoned his policy of selecting a more recognised ball-player at inside centre with Llewellyn named in the 12 jersey.

Fly-half Sam Costelow is preferred to Dan Edwards, while wings Josh Adams and Louis Rees-Zammit and full-back Blair Murray form the back three.

Props Nicky Smith and Archie Griffin start alongside captain Dewi Lake, while Dafydd Jenkins has shaken off a knee injury to resume his Six Nations partnership with Ben Carter. Alex Mann, Jac Morgan and Aaron Wainwright form the back row.

Tandy has made seven personnel changes from the side that lost 43-0 against South Africa in July.

Nine of the 15 starters against Japan, including six of the eight forwards, and 12 of the 23-strong squad, play club rugby in England.

There are three Scarlets players, two from Cardiff, one Dragon and no Ospreys, although half-backs Edwards and Reuben Morgan-Williams have been named as replacements.

"There's lots of competition for positions within the squad, which is where we want to be," said Tandy.

How will Wales fare on Nations Championship return?

Morgan aims to show new attacking threat for Wales

This will be Tandy's sixth different centre partnership in his 13th international in charge, with Joe Hawkins or Ben Thomas having being given the number 12 jersey in the previous 12 internationals.

Thomas and Llewellyn were the Wales duo that started against South Africa in July.

Thomas is missing because of a calf injury while Hawkins has been left out of the 23-strong squad for the autumn games.

Llewellyn played most of his early senior rugby for Cardiff at inside centre before leaving for Gloucester, where he has played more at outside centre alongside England midfield-man Seb Atkinson at Kingsholm.

Before the start of the season, Llewellyn told BBC Sport Wales inside centre was his preferred position.

He has only worn the number 12 shirt for Gloucester on one occasion this season, and started just once at inside centre for Wales in a World Cup warm-up game against England in August 2023.

James has also came though the Scarlets as a more natural 12 but Tandy says he sees the Wales future of the 24-year-old from Carmarthen at 13.

"We're excited to see the pairing," said Tandy.

"We've had a couple of training sessions together, and it's been really good to watch.

"There's strong competition, and you can't overlook Max's form since returning.

"He also had a run at number 12 against Bath, His defensive performances have been excellent, but he can also play with the ball.

"He's played at inside centre regularly for Cardiff, so we're confident he can deliver what we're looking for.

"So we're looking forward to seeing what the partnership can produce."

Wales return to Nations Championship action

Wales started the Nations Championship campaign in July with a victory against Fiji before defeats against Argentina and South Africa.

After resuming the campaign against Japan, Wales will host New Zealand and Australia in successive Saturdays before travelling to the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham on the final weekend of November to face yet unknown opposition in the play-off games.

"We're excited to be to back at home," said Tandy.

"We want to go out there on Saturday, put our mark on the match and start the next phase in our Nations Championship campaign strongly."

Wales and Japan both currently lie fifth in their respective hemisphere tables.

In July, Japan beat Italy but lost to Ireland and France in the opening three games of the tournament.

Wales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, James, Llewellyn, Adams; Costelow, Tomos Williams; Smith, Lake (capt), Griffin, Jenkins, Carter, Mann, Morgan, Wainwright.

Replacements: Elias, Carre, Francis, Teddy Williams, Botham, Morgan-Williams, D Edwards, Hennessey.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Tara Jones - how England international became a referee
articles.summary: Four years ago, Tara Jones played in a Rugby League World Cup semi-final for England. This Saturday, she will be refereeing one.
articles.body:
Four years ago, Tara Jones played for England in a Rugby League World Cup semi-final.

This Saturday, she will be refereeing one, when New Zealand's women - her opponents in 2022 - face Samoa in Newcastle, New South Wales.

It means that the former St Helens hooker has gone one stage further at the tournament than either England's men or women managed this time around.

She has come a long way since starting out as a referee, where the tests of character came from the very beginning - in one of her earliest games, when she was aged just 12, she had to send off a misbehaving parent on the sideline.

For years, she combined officiating with a successful playing career at Saints, with whom she won a Women's Super League title, two League Leaders' Shields and four Challenge Cups - becoming the first woman to score a try in a Challenge Cup final at Wembley, in 2023, a year before her retirement.

Still only 30, Jones has been made an MBE for her services to a sport in which she made history in March by becoming the first woman to referee a men's Super League fixture.

As RFL match officials department general manager Andy Smith put it when her semi-final appointment was announced on Tuesday, Jones "is building a reputation as one of the world's top officials".

She has come a long way since her start in the sport, when she had to show a stubborn streak just to stay involved - which was a major factor in her taking up refereeing in the first place.

Jones, who is officiating in her first major international tournament, has taken charge of three games at the Women's World Cup so far - including one involving some of her former international team-mates.

She was in the was in the middle for England's 70-6 victory over Wales on 17 October, before refereeing two France matches, against New Zealand and Fiji.

And she has documented all the time and work she has put in behind the scenes at the World Cup on her Instagram account.

Born in Germany - where her father was serving in the Army at the time - and raised in Warrington, Jones has been on quite the sporting journey.

It began as a young girl being taken to rugby training by her dad - ignoring her mother's desire for her to take up dance.

"My brother played and my dad took him training - he was the team manager. I was probably that annoying little kid who was trying to join in but getting in the way a little bit," she told BBC Radio Merseyside in March.

"My mum wouldn't let me play because I was her little girl, and I think she wanted me to be a dancer. I was never going to be a dancer... or ballet, or gymnastics, or something like that. My dad secretly took my across to my own age group and let me play.

"Unfortunately, when I got to the end of Under-11s, I was then told I couldn't carry on. Back then, the opportunities for girls to play rugby were few and far between.

"It's much better now. But that's why I went into officiating. I was a bit stubborn, and I was told that I couldn't do something within the sport that I loved.

"I was like: Well, I will find a different avenue, and no-one's going to tell me I can't be involved in this sport at the top level and within the boys' side of it."

Rugby League World Cup: New Zealand v Samoa

Listen to live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app

Jones has hardly looked back, having only joined the RFL match officials department on a full-time basis two years ago.

She is one of three UK-based officials at the World Cup, alongside Liam Moore and Chris Kendall.

And having faced the Kiwi Ferns on a dark and dank night in York four years ago, she is likely to have much happier memories of this semi-final - and the fortitude to brush aside any negative social media comments surrounding her appointment.

"I remember at 12 years of age sending off a parent who was stood on the sideline. You've got to have broad shoulders and stick up for yourself," she added.

"I was probably a bit shy as a kid as well, to be honest, and not really out there. But put me on a rugby field and I'm just a different person. Over time, that confidence has grown within me off the field as well, and it's made me the person that I am.

"So it's definitely given me those attributes and life skills as I've been growing up.

"I hope I can inspire young girls - and match officials in general. It's a bonus if I can get young girls into the sport.

"I've had parents say to me: I tell my little girl about everything you've achieved, because I want her to look up to you, and be like you, and know there are opportunities for her to do that.

"On a personal level, my own nephew, who is seven, said to his dad, 'There's Auntie Tara on the news,' when I was receiving my MBE. 'I want to be like Tara.'

"That was a really special moment when I got told my own nephew aspires to be like me and wants to go on and achieve big things."

articles.title: Nations Championship: Wales turn to English-based players for Japan match
articles.summary: With a record number of players based outside of Wales in his 23-man squad, head coach Steve Tandy says how they are playing is all that matters.
articles.body:
Head coach Steve Tandy says he does not consider which clubs his players play for when he selects his Wales side.

Tandy has named 12 players from English clubs in his squad for the Nations Championship match against Japan in Cardiff, with nine in the starting XV, including six forwards.

It is understood to be a record number of players based outside of Wales in a 23-man squad.

"I just see the boys playing the best at the minute and also you put in what fits to how we want to play," said Tandy.

"Ultimately it doesn't matter where they play, it'll be the best players.

"It's never about where they play, it's more about who are playing the best rugby."

Wales opt for centre power pair against Japan

The Prem talents hunting Wales breakthroughs

Gloucester trio Dewi Lake, Jac Morgan and Max Llewellyn, join Louis Rees-Zammit (Bristol), Tomos Williams (Saracens), Nicky Smith (Sale), Archie Griffin (Bath), Dafydd Jenkins (Exeter) and Aaron Wainwright (Leicester), along with three more Prem players on the bench in Tomas Francis (Sale), Rhys Carre (Saracens) and Louis Hennessey (Bath).

It represents a significant shift since a rule - which stopped players with fewer than 60 caps being eligible if they played outside Wales - was changed in February 2023 to set the bar at just 25 caps.

Only six England-based players were in a 33-man Wales squad at the 2023 World Cup.

Tandy believes the number of non Wales-based players is an indication other leagues want Welsh talent, and that they are performing at the highest level when they go to new clubs.

"They're also experiencing different environments and receiving different stimulus.

"They're coming back with different experiences, things they've learned and plenty of motivation to represent Wales."

Tandy accepts there are logistical challenges to preparation time, with England-based players returning to their clubs for certain periods when players at Welsh regions are available to work with him.

"We have to make the best of the situation," said Tandy.

"I'd love to have more players based in Wales, that would be fantastic but that's not the situation at the moment.

"You have to keep an open mind. We can either complain about having 20 players playing overseas, or we can recognise the benefits."

The Wales coach accepts that brings a mix of positives, and some things he may potentially lose.

"We might not have as much contact with those players or be able to bring them into alignment camps as regularly," he added.

"However, some are playing in front of full stadiums every week and experiencing different styles of competition and coaching."

Tandy left Wales in 2018 for coaching experiences in Australia and Scotland before returning as national head coach in 2025.

"That's part of the benefit, you go somewhere else and discover new things," he said.

"From my own personal experience of going outside Wales, I learned a great deal.

"When I moved from Wales to Australia, I also had to learn different things away from the field.

"You learn more about yourself, how to look after yourself and how to prepare properly."

Lake and Morgan joined Gloucester from Ospreys, while Wainwright has linked up with Leicester.

"I think there's definitely a change in them," said Tandy.

"There's something new, like it drags your attention, as you're on a little bit more of an edge or there's tension or excitement.

"So going to new environments generally do raise that anyway because you want to go into environments and perform.

"Seeing different things and then being around some English internationals will have been great."

Tandy highlighted the experience of Wainwright, who since his move from Dragons in the summer has helped Leicester to the top of the English Prem.

"Probably playing in Leicester with sellout crowds and the challenge of working with people like Ollie Chessum, who has been on British and Irish Lions tours, the standard goes up again.

"It gives them confidence, they realise how good some of the Welsh players are.

"That's not typically Welsh either, it's probably seeing what you could be as well."

Morgan aims to show new attacking threat for Wales

Wales players in Prem doing nation proud - Smith

Tandy says despite players making their living across the border he is able to stay in contact.

"That includes travelling to see them and having phone conversations," he explained.

"Gloucester and Bath are also relatively close to Cardiff, so we can maintain those relationships throughout the year, not just during international campaigns.

"I also speak regularly with their head coaches to understand how they're progressing, where they're performing well and which areas they need to develop."

He says it is about showing players that the national set-up cares about them, their development and environment.

"We discuss their rugby, what they're learning and whether they need additional support.

"Once they return to the national environment, we can challenge them more effectively because we understand where they are."

articles.title: England v Australia: Behind Twickenham's high-tech new turf
articles.summary: England's men will be playing on a revolutionary new surface when they take on the Wallabies on Sunday.
articles.body:
Nobody is keener than Jim Buttar to see flowing, running rugby at Twickenham this autumn.

"A 58-52 scoreline, one scrum and three line-outs all match, and we'll go home happy!" he tells BBC Sport.

Buttar's interest is professional though, rather than just the pleasure of the game.

He is England Rugby's head of grounds and technical operations, in charge of the Allianz Stadium turf.

"When the ball is in hand more and the game is more flowing and open, the wear and tear on the surface is a bit more spread out," he says.

However the action unfolds, Buttar and his team will be busy.

England play Australia on Sunday, before matches against Japan and New Zealand on 14 and 21 November respectively.

Those will be full-on days, primping and preening the playing surface. The final weekend of November, though, will be something else.

The Nations Championship finals take place at Allianz Stadium from 27 to 29 November, with double-header fixtures involving the top 12 Test teams in the world on three successive days.

"We are likely to be doing 14 or 15-hour days and that is just what it is," says Buttar.

"That finals weekend is a very condensed number of high-pressure games in a short space of time, but I'm actually looking forward to it, being able to really test yourself and all the planning that you've done."

Over the summer, the Allianz Stadium surface was relaid.

The turf that Buttar and his team had tended with such care since 2012 was unceremoniously ripped up, with diggers lifting out 9,500 tonnes of earth and grass.

Rolls of new turf, each one 11 metres long and a little over a metre wide, were laid in four days.

Grown and harvested 200 miles away, the turf was transported from Scunthorpe to London to take centre stage at English rugby's home.

The previous pitch depended on a sand base to drain water. Moisture would pass through the turf and down the drain quickly, ensuring that, even after a deluge, the pitch would be playable.

However, such a system has disadvantages. Any nutrition applied to the grass also had little time to work, passing through and away before the full benefits could take effect.

Environmentally and financially, with the price of fertilisers rocketing in recent years, Buttar knew better was possible.

A fact-finding trip to the Netherlands prompted the installation of a huge hi-tech reservoir, capable of holding 1.4 million litres of water below the pitch.

It essentially enables Buttar to mechanically move the water table, either speeding up or slowing down moisture's passage through the turf depending on whether drainage or nutrition is the priority.

Water is also captured so it can be reused, with nanobubble technology - aerating with miniscule bubbles to bolster soil health and turf durability and avoid stagnation - helping to keep it fresh enough for reapplication.

"We were looking for a more sustainable way of doing all things, while still being able to produce a world-class surface," says Buttar.

A week after the pitch was put in place, England women christened it with a dramatic win over New Zealand in September.

When Buttar and his team assessed the surface afterwards, they found that their new surface, which is 93% natural and 7% plastic yarn, compared to a 97%/3% mix previously, was sturdier than before.

There are too many variables to get too comfortable, however.

"For the best part of four or five months of the year, we're dancing with the devil in terms of the weather," said Buttar.

"We know it's going to be wet for a period, we know it's going to be cold, but we don't know when exactly.

"We just have to do our best to understand the forecast as well as possible, make sure we've got a plan A, B, C, and D and just adjust as the weather changes.

"It can be as simple as a weather front passing within two miles of the stadium changing everything."

There are also more leftfield concerns to nag Buttar.

He has extensive protocols in place to ensure that the sprinkler system doesn't activate mid-match, as has happened at other grounds.

In a previous role, in charge of Tottenham's White Hart Lane surface, Buttar arrived on a matchday morning to find a malfunctioning sprinkle head had blown a metre-wide hole in the centre circle.

His hurried stitching of new turf and cosmetic touch-ups were completed just in time to go undetected by television cameras.

At Twickenham, the local wildlife poses a challenge.

"There is a fairly decent urban fox population," says Buttar.

"Post-match, as quickly as the cleaners can get everything cleaned up and get all the food waste away, they're going to come in roaming.

"Sometimes the foxes will get their fill and then bury some for later.

"We've found half-eaten burgers, pies and bits and pieces dug into the pitch.

"Once we found an egg, perfect, with no damage whatsoever, which a fox had carefully put in a little hole and covered back up."

Egg-burying or egg-chasing, it all now happens on one of the highest-tech surfaces in the world.

articles.title: Ireland v Argentina: Talk of Irish rugby's decline 'nonsense', says Dan Sheehan
articles.summary: Ireland captain Dan Sheehan says he has "full confidence" in his team-mates as he dismissed talk of a decline in Irish rugby as "nonsense".
articles.body:
Ireland captain Dan Sheehan says he has "full confidence" in his team-mates as he dismissed talk of a decline in Irish rugby as "nonsense".

Andy Farrell's side sit third in the world rankings, but a string of double-digit losses to South Africa, New Zealand and France have raised question marks about the team's trajectory.

Farrell this week admitted his team are not yet ready to have realistic ambitions of winning next year's World Cup in Australia.

But before facing Argentina, Fiji and world champions South Africa at home in this month's Nations Championship fixtures, Sheehan insisted Ireland must "fully back ourselves".

"I've full confidence in this group," said Sheehan, who is again deputising for injured skipper Caelan Doris this month.

"I think reminding myself and the group of the quality we have...sometimes you can hear outside noise about, 'is this a transitioning time for Irish rugby?' or 'is this a decline in Irish rugby?' and I think it's all nonsense really.

"Making sure we keep our confidence in what we have, in the personnel we have, the coaches we have in the group, it's all set up perfectly for us. I think it's just doubling down on our work ethic and making sure we fully back ourselves."

Ireland must step up for World Cup countdown - Farrell

Casey, Jansen and Timoney start against Argentina

Jansen targets regular starts ahead of home debut

Ireland have won six out of their eight Tests this year, including convincing wins over England and Scotland that helped seal the Six Nations Triple Crown.

However, a 36-14 loss to France in Paris and July's 40-21 reverse to the All Blacks exposed the shortcomings in Farrell's side, with Sheehan admitting improvement is needed "across a lot of areas".

"We've been disappointed with a fair few performances that we've had, especially the big opportunities we had over the summer," added the 28-year-old Leinster hooker.

"The Australia game, I know we scraped a win but it probably wasn't a performance we wanted. And the same with Eden Park [against New Zealand], I think we were beaten by about 20.

"Obviously, set-piece is something we need to continue to drive. I think we have the ability in the group. You see it in the provinces, it's a quality set-piece we have and we need to make sure we drive that at international level but there's plenty."

Live commentary on BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sport website and app

Sheehan added that while Ireland have a "few things to tidy up", he does not feel the side are a "million miles off" where they need to be.

"I thought the focus over the last two weeks has been great – honest feedback, honest conversations with each other about where we're at and where we need to be.

"I think we can all feel we have the talent in the group, and we're going in the right direction if we can put all of our minds together."

Sheehan also expects a tough opening assignment against Argentina on Friday night as the Pumas chase a first away win over Ireland at the 12th attempt - having beaten Farrell's British and Irish Lions at the Aviva Stadium last year.

"All eyes will be on this game and they're a top-quality side that put the Lions away here so we know the threat they have, the passion they have for the game as well," said Sheehan.

"I'm sure they'll be coming out all guns blazing and we need to match that and take it to a different level."

articles.title: Eddie Jones: The smiling wind-up merchant who refuses to fade away
articles.summary: You never know whether you will get a compliment, a cutting observation, verbal grenade or all three from mischievous Eddie Jones.
articles.body:
An Eddie Jones press conference has always been an event in itself.

You never quite know what is coming. A compliment, a cutting observation, a verbal grenade. Sometimes all three, invariably delivered with that mischievous smile.

Jones belongs to a disappearing generation of coaches who understood that the contest could begin long before the players took the field.

Warren Gatland could intimidate with his imposing presence and gruff demeanour alone. Jose Mourinho proclaimed himself 'The Special One' and made confrontation an art form.

Jones was different. Small in stature, with an almost permanent grin, he could stir up an entire nation while thoroughly enjoying himself.

All three built reputations on dominance. Not simply on the pitch, but over the agenda, their players and the organisations they represented.

But the language of coaching is changing.

Wales head coach Steve Tandy talks about connection and relationships. Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler emphasises collaboration, trust and understanding the person behind the player.

Neither lacks ambition or authority, but their approach contrasts with the era of the all-powerful head coach.

At 66, Jones remains one of rugby's most fascinating characters from that old school.

In 2018 Jones questioned whether Wales fly-half Rhys Patchell could handle the pressure of playing England at Twickenham, while describing Warren Gatland's team as "confident and cocky".

But his provocations sometimes crossed the line.

That same year Jones apologised after footage emerged of him using some choice language to describe Wales and Ireland in less than flattering terms at a sponsor's event the previous year.

The former was classic Jones. Identify a weakness, plant a seed of doubt and ensure everyone was talking about it. The latter showed when the wind-ups went too far.

Speaking to BBC Sport prior to Japan's Nations Championship meeting with Wales, Jones offered an intriguing explanation.

"Some of them were planned to an extent. Others might have come out of the press conference. Sometimes you say things at the press conference that you don't mean to say. But, yeah, sometimes."

Players picked on form not club location - Tandy

Jones looks to create Japan history in Cardiff

"And particularly with England, I always felt with the English that they didn't have enough confidence in themselves."

Jones explained that part of his responsibility was to provide that self-belief.

"So I felt one of my roles was to give them that confidence, to be almost the battering ram for them."

For Jones, the mind games served more than one purpose. Unsettling opponents was one thing, but taking pressure off his players was just as important.

And if that meant making himself the centre of attention, so be it.

An extraordinary workaholic, he is renowned for his almost impossible standards. Players have described receiving messages from him at 3am while he was exercising, only to be questioned at breakfast about why they had not replied.

Yet even as an international coach, Jones has been known to quietly turn up at local clubs to coach minis, or drive hours to a player's testimonial dinner without a fee.

His career has had its extremes. England dismissed him in 2022, while his return to Australia ended with the Wallabies' first pool-stage exit at the 2023 World Cup.

In Lyon, after Australia had been thrashed by Wales, the familiar grin was absent. Jones was prickly, irritated and facing questions about his future.

Three years on, as he looked forward to Japan facing Wales in Cardiff in the Nations Championship on Saturday, the contrast was striking. Relaxed, charming and generous with his answers, he appeared to be thoroughly enjoying himself.

For all his contradictions, Jones remains a rugby obsessive. Nothing illustrated that better than his answer when asked which Welsh player had left the greatest impression on him.

Not Gareth Edwards, Shane Williams or Alun Wyn Jones, but Liam Williams, the former Wales and British and Irish Lions full-back renowned for his bravery under the high ball.

"Every time I come to Millennium Stadium (sic), I have this picture of Liam Williams winning box kicks," Jones told the Scrum V podcast.

"He was all elbows and knees, but he could do something brilliant in the game."

It was a rugby purist's answer. An appreciation of the finer details rather than simply the most celebrated names.

That affection for the finer details extends to Welsh rugby more broadly.

Jones spoke warmly of Cardiff's Principality Stadium and praised Steve Tandy's rebuilding work, particularly the leadership of Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan.

But the old competitive instincts remain.

Japan's coach knows the value of silencing the Cardiff crowd, and believes a strong start could turn Welsh supporters' frustrations into a psychological advantage.

Even the charming, reflective Jones is still searching for an edge.

As the conversation ended, he offered encouragement to Welsh supporters.

"So, yeah, for the Welsh supporters, just keep backing your team."

"But don't back them too much on Saturday."

articles.title: Fixtures and standings as Nations Championship returns
articles.summary: What is the Nations Championship, who is winning and who plays who this weekend?
articles.body:
The Nations Championship resumes on Friday with Ireland taking on Argentina in Dublin, as the battle for continental supremacy heats up.

After three rounds of home games for southern hemisphere nations in July, the northern hemisphere teams are the hosts for the final three rounds.

Six Nations champions France, who play Fiji on Saturday, head the standings in the north with 12 points, and as things stand would play world champions South Africa in the inaugural final at Allianz Stadium on 29 November.

But with France set to host South Africa on Friday, 13 November, before taking on Argentina on 21 November, that could all change.

Scotland are one point behind Les Bleus but face a tricky match against New Zealand - a team they have never beaten - at Murrayfield on Saturday before games against Australia and Japan.

Third-placed England have 10 points and play Australia - who are third in the southern standings - at Allianz Stadium on Sunday before taking on Japan and New Zealand.

Ireland, who also have 10 points, face the challenge of taking on South Africa in the final round after playing Fiji in their second home game.

Wales beat Fiji before losing to Argentina and South Africa in their opening three matches. Their home games are against Japan, New Zealand and Australia.

Bottom-side Italy lost all three of their away games and face South Africa on Saturday.

The Springboks beat England, Scotland and Wales at home in their opening three Tests to lead New Zealand on points difference.

The Nations Championship pits the northern hemisphere teams who compete in the Six Nations - England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy - against southern hemisphere giants South Africa, New Zealand, Australia and Argentina, plus invited sides Fiji and Japan.

All teams will play each of the six in the opposing hemisphere once, with three rounds of fixtures staged in July and another three in November.

Their results will rank the teams within their own hemisphere, from one to six.

On the final weekend in November, there is a three-day play-off event staged at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham. The sixth-placed team in the northern hemisphere plays off against the equivalent in the southern hemisphere standings and so on, culminating in the two top-ranked sides taking each other on.

The winner of that final match is crowned the inaugural Nations Championship winner.

There is also a parallel, Ryder-Cup style hemisphere title. The winner of each of the matches on the play-offs weekend will earn one point for their hemisphere, except for the contest between the two top-ranked teams which delivers two.

The first hemisphere to earn four points over the weekend will be crowned winners.

articles.title: Scotland can be best and worst team in world - Jack Dempsey says before New Zealand Test
articles.summary: Jack Dempsey on his guilt over leaving Glasgow, coming up against Dave Rennie and Scotland's hopes of finally overcoming New Zealand.
articles.body:
It's the question that has fried the brain and torn at the heart of every Scottish rugby fan - what does this team have to do to crash through the glass ceiling they have been hopping their heads against for the longest time?

On Saturday, at Murrayfield, they have another shot at the All Blacks - the 34th. They have had three near misses in a row under Gregor Townsend. Three wasted opportunities to beat the Kiwis for the first time ever.

"There's no magic pill," says Jack Dempsey, recently of Glasgow Warriors but now of Toshiba Brave Lupus in Japan. Dempsey is a straight talker. When you ask what needs to happen for Scotland to turn a corner once and for all, he does not mess about for long.

"It's probably two things," says the number eight. "Number one is momentum. There's momentum within games. We can be the best team in the world for 20 minutes and we can be the worst team in the world for 20 minutes.

"The Springboks are the flavour of the last eight years or so. They have a team that shows up every week and delivers and then they have a second team that does the same thing.

"The second thing is messaging. Can we stay stronger together for longer? That's what Sione [Tuipulotu] has been preaching. And what that means is, from a defensive point of view, can we make the team against us earn every single phase? Can we make it harder for them on every single phase?

"And then on attack, every time we hold the ball, we make it harder for the opposition. Can we do that on another level?

"If we just keep stacking those moments the habits will change. And then the results should follow."

Scotland face more ambitious All Blacks - Townsend

No end in sight for Russell as he eyes famous All Blacks win

Dempsey will play his 50th Test on Saturday - he has 14 for the Wallabies and this will be number 36 for Scotland.

Based in Japan, he's available for all of the Nations Championship, unavailable for all of the Six Nations and then available again for the World Cup. That move to Japan, after five years with Glasgow, was one he thought about long and hard.

His mind was ever-changing when he was weighing it up, he says. He admits to feeling a little guilt over leaving the club that "resurrected" his career. Then there was the prospect of missing the Six Nations.

"You can be playing the Six Nations and be like 'this is the greatest thing, winning a Calcutta Cup'," he says. "All the other games as well, but mainly that one. You're like 'I'd love to drink from this cup every single year for the rest of my life'.

"I'd wake up one day and change my mind, wake up the next day and change it again. For me, it just came down to the cliche of only having one career. Let's try and do as much as you can.

"I've been so lucky to play Super Rugby, played for my home country, played for Glasgow and then played at Murrayfield. One thing I've learned in my career is that Murrayfield is the best place to play rugby, without a doubt.

"Every time you go to Murrayfield and play a game it's like it's your first one. You want to make sure that you don't take that for granted."

He will meet Dave Rennie again on Saturday. "We've had a chequered past," smiles Dempsey of the now New Zealand head coach.

Rennie didn't much fancy Dempsey when he was coaching Australia, describing the back row as lacking in physicality, something that could not be said of him in recent years.

"I wasn't in a great spot in Australia when he came in and gave me a kick up the arse, which sent me to Glasgow," Dempsey explains. "So in a way, you know, it really helped me.

"He's a pretty straight shooter, straight down the barrel. He'll give you some hard truths. He's a high-character guy, a highly successful guy. There's no bitterness there."

Saturday, he stresses, is all about those pressure moments and Scotland's ability to make life hell for Rennie's All Blacks.

"Not everyone gets what they deserve and not everyone gets what they should," Dempsey says.

Every win is hard-earned. A win against the All Blacks especially so.

More than 120 years since they first played the tourists, the chance has come again to beat them. The near-misses don't count for anything more.

Podcast: Can Scotland end 121 years of history against All Blacks?

articles.title: Nations Championship: Ireland's home straight to World Cup 2027 starts with Argentina visit
articles.summary: Less than a year away from a potential 2027 World Cup quarter-final meeting, Ireland's hosting of Argentina represents an important staging post on the journey to Australia next autumn.
articles.body:
Los Pumas - two words to strike fear into the heart of Ireland rugby fans.

As they return to the Aviva Stadium in the Nations Championship on Friday night, it feels something of an anomaly that a team who have inflicted so much hurt on Ireland over the years have never beaten them in Dublin.

Indeed, out of the 20 previous meetings between these two sides, Ireland have won 14. It is the nature of those handful of losses, however, that have so coloured this rivalry.

Three times the sides have met at the World Cup.

Three times Argentina have won and three times the result has heralded Ireland's early exit from the competition.

With Ireland's first game of Australia 2027 now just under 11 months away, the sight of the blue and white hoops of their frequent tournament nemesis will certainly sharpen the mind.

All the more so given that, should results go in accordance with seeding, the sides would meet at the quarter-final stage on Halloween night in Brisbane.

Live commentary on BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sport website and app

As he announced his team selection on Wednesday afternoon, Ireland head coach Andy Farrell acknowledged his side are not presently "good enough to board the plane believing that 100%" they are ready to lift the Webb Ellis trophy for the first time.

A year out from the World Cups of 2015, 2019 and 2023, Ireland had enjoyed banner seasons, and by this stage were eagerly anticipating the tournaments to come.

While that has not been the case through 2026 to date, the head coach added that he is excited by the thought of the work still to do.

If wider optimism around next year feels in short supply, it is because Ireland's issues have come to bear when playing the very best.

Across the past two years, their only six defeats have come in the six games they have played against New Zealand, South Africa and France. All came via double-digit scores.

As such, the eye has long been drawn to the visit of the Springboks to Dublin on 21 November, but there can be no looking past a dangerous Argentina fixture.

The Pumas will be expected to provide a good yardstick for both the collective and a number of individuals in an intriguing selection.

With Jack Crowley injured, Sam Prendergast has another opportunity to grab the 10 jersey. When the then 21-year-old made his debut in this fixture two years ago, it certainly felt like a selection with the future, and the 2027 World Cup, in mind.

The Leinster player has had an uneven start to his Test career, and had lost his place in even his provincial 23 by the time of last season's Champions Cup final, but has the chance to lay down a real marker this month.

Farrell has also put his faith in two regular bench options from the start.

For all the talk of Prendergast's readiness to be Johnny Sexton's long-term successor at fly-half, the now assistant coach's role as the backline's cerebral fulcrum has already been assumed by Jamison Gibson-Park.

Arguably Ireland's most important player during this World Cup cycle, the scrum-half missed the start of the season with a groin injury but was player of the match in his return against Munster at the Aviva Stadium.

He will start this window on the bench with Craig Casey instead getting the nod. The 27-year-old will win his 31st cap on Friday but will be making just a second start against a side currently in the top eight of the world rankings.

It is a similar story for Nick Timoney, preferred here to Josh van der Flier, who has become a trusted bench option over the past 12 months but gets a start against this level of opposition for the first time.

Without Caelan Doris and Jack Conan through injury, how the Ulster flanker, Sean Jansen and Ryan Baird fare against what is an abrasive Argentina back row should have a big impact on the game.

How 'student of coaching' Contepomi took unexpected path

Jack Conan on the Ireland Rugby Social - Lions, Leinster and learnings

Schmidt still proving 'very bad at retiring'

While United Rugby Championship results for Irish sides this season have been poor - the provinces have combined for just six wins, three of them by Leinster - key players should at least be more battle-hardened than a year ago.

Then, with so many coming off the British and Irish Lions tour of Australia last summer, most had only one game under their belt when looking so flat during their defeat by New Zealand in Chicago. Now, at least, many frontliners have featured in multiple club games before making the jump back to Test-level rugby.

Argentina, however, certainly seem more primed than they have been for recent windows too.

Head coach Felipe Contepomi has spoken of historic significance of chasing a first away win over Ireland, even if 12 of his matchday squad have recent fond memories of the Aviva Stadium from their win over the Lions there 17 months ago.

The side have lost 12 of 18 Tests since that famous win, although Contepomi, like so many of his predecessors, has had difficulties with player availability as a southern hemisphere team whose squad is mainly based in the north.

While there are absentees for this tour - most notably Bath's Santiago Carreras and Lyon prop Thomas Gallo - the 12 changes made from the 28-28 draw with Australia in September undoubtedly have strengthened a starting side with 750 caps' worth of Test experience.

Coupled with the addition of Shaun Edwards and Mario Ledesma to Contepomi's coaching staff, Los Pumas feel more than capable of giving Ireland exactly the sort of challenge needed as the World Cup looms ever closer on the horizon.

articles.title: RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney confirms WRU approach for Anglo-Welsh league
articles.summary: RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney confirms the WRU has officially asked to join an Anglo-Welsh league, although no talks have taken place.
articles.body:
Rugby Football Union (RFU) chief executive Bill Sweeney has confirmed the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) has officially asked to join the English Prem and form an Anglo-Welsh league.

The Prem hopes to expand from 10 to 12 teams for the 2029-30 season, with a "long-term ambition" to grow further.

Wales have four professional sides, Ospreys, Cardiff, Scarlets and Dragons, that currently play in the 16-team United Rugby Championship (URC), although the WRU has plans to cut one of those four teams.

Welsh rugby's governing body, along with the other national unions which includes teams from Scotland, Ireland, Italy and South Africa, are stakeholders in that league.

Now the RFU says the WRU has asked to be part of an Anglo-Welsh tournament.

"We have received a formal approach," Sweeney told BBC Radio Four.

"We asked for that and we wanted it in writing. We wanted to understand a few points and that has been submitted to us."

Prem reluctant to commit on Anglo-Welsh league

RFU committed to English expansion in Prem

Three sides, Worcester, Wasps and London Irish, were forced to fold during the 2022-23 season when the Premiership - as it was then known - was reduced to 10 teams.

Traditional promotion and relegation to and from the top tier was scrapped from the start of the 2026-27 season after landmark changes to English rugby were voted through.

Instead of earning a play-off shot at replacing the Prem's bottom side by finishing top of the second-tier Champ and meeting the top flight's minimum standards, clubs will instead apply to join and be judged across a range of criteria.

Bids will be assessed on standard of play, finances, investment potential, infrastructure and how their geographical base could help spread the Prem's appeal, among other factors.

Conditions were initially set that any team wanting to play in the Prem will need to complete a campaign in the Champ before being considered.

Sweeney has reaffirmed his commitment to expanding the English game, with no formal talks having yet taken place with their Welsh counterparts.

"Our primary focus is on the expansion of the English game," said Sweeney.

"We have had some developments there recently with no longer having an automatic promotion or relegation but having an expansion game.

"Financial criteria, fan base, geographical location, ability on the field of play, will determine whether you can get into the Prem or not.

"We see that as a way of expanding the 10 teams and our focus is on expanding the English game.

"But we have been approached [by the WRU] and it is responsible for us to go back and ask more questions."

Those questions will be answers about what is happening in the chaotic state of the Welsh domestic game.

The WRU is currently in the middle of cutting the number of Welsh professional teams from four to three by 2028.

The governing body has announced it will award licences to Cardiff and Dragons, pitting Ospreys and Scarlets against each other for the west Wales licence with a final decision expected by the summer of 2027.

New WRU chair Lyndon Faulkner came in and suggested he will look at everything, including keeping four professional sides, while he indicated he was a fan of an Anglo-Welsh tournament.

Now the WRU is trying to get a possible two sides into an Anglo-Welsh tournament, which was the number of professional teams the Union initially wanted to maintain when its reduction policy started.

The URC has been contacted by the BBC to see whether the WRU would face any legal action over lobbying to join another league, as it has committed to providing four sides to the current URC competition for another two years.

"There are some fundamental questions there," said Sweeney.

"We don't yet have a clear understanding of how they would legally exit the URC which they are a member of, so that has to be clarified in some detail.

"Going into cross-border competition has different ramifications and we have to be clear around the complexities."

When approached after Sweeney's comments, the WRU referred to a statement made last week: "Welsh men's professional teams compete in the URC and the WRU is committed to providing four teams to the URC until the end of the 2027-28 season.

"By the end of this season, the WRU will have determined the future operating model for the men's game in Wales.

"The WRU will continue to work with other shareholders in the URC on future Welsh representation in the competition.

"The WRU keeps under review the competition opportunities which may be available across the game and could be in the best interests of Welsh rugby.

"The idea of Anglo-Welsh competitions is something often debated by Welsh rugby fans.

"The WRU understands the appeal of the English top flight, which is why we are pitching for two of our women's teams, Brython Thunder and Gwalia Lightning, to be included in Premiership Women's Rugby."

articles.title: England v Australia: Ollie Chessum on captaincy links
articles.summary: Ollie Chessum says that he relishes being an on-pitch leader after being tipped as a long-term successor to England skipper Maro Itoje.
articles.body:
Ollie Chessum says that he relishes being an on-pitch leader after being tipped as a long-term successor to England skipper Maro Itoje.

Chessum, who captains Prem table-toppers Leicester and toured Australia with the British and Irish Lions last year, has become a key part of England's pack, able to operate in both the second row and at blindside flanker.

"While it's nice that people can tickle your ego a little bit and give you that compliment and I do really enjoy the leadership side of the game, it's certainly not one for now," Chessum told BBC Radio 5 Live Breakfast.

"It is maybe further down the line that I have leadership ambitions, but I feel like captaincy is not really something you go after. I feel like it's a role that almost finds the right individual.

"Right now we've got a very, very good captain in Maro and I'm picking his brains as part of an incredibly experienced senior leadership group.

"Who knows what's down the line in years to come? Of course, it would be a pretty special thing to do, I'm sure."

Itoje, 32, was appointed as England captain in January 2025, taking over the role from Saracens team-mate Jamie George.

Owen Farrell previously held the full-time role since 2019, before stepping back from Test rugby in late 2023 and then moving to France, becoming ineligible for international selection.

Chessum, 26, says there has been no issue smoothing over the ructions that have occurred between him and England team-mates on club duty in recent weeks.

He was at the centre of a half-time skirmish in Tigers' win over East Midlands rivals Northampton, pushing Henry Pollock down the tunnel, before briefly confronting Bristol's Ellis Genge a week later.

"It's not difficult at all [to put all that behind you]," Chessum said. "They are two of my close mates in camp.

"Gengey is someone I've known for a number of years since he was my captain at Leicester and Henry's obviously someone I've got to know very well the last couple of years.

"Gengey was captain for the year we managed to win the Premiership under Steve [Borthwick].

"It is strange coming up against him in a different shirt but I'd expect nothing less of Gengey than to try and get under your skin somehow. It's all part of the game. He loves it. You see the smile on his face as he's walking away from you in that game.

"I'd expect nothing less of them and they'd I'd hope would expect nothing less of me than to give 100% for whatever shirt I'm wearing."

England take on Australia on Sunday as they return to Allianz Stadium for the first time since February's 42-21 defeat by Ireland, one of the lowlights of a miserable Six Nations campaign.

England lost to world champions South Africa in July, before wins over Fiji and Argentina.

Live commentary on BBC Sports Extra, BBC Sport website and app

Chessum says he understands that patience among the Twickenham patrons may be wearing thin.

"I can totally understand the frustration because we as a group feel it," he said.

"We've got a huge amount of talent in the room. We've got an incredible coaching set-up who couldn't really give us any more. We're constantly trying to improve and find ways, but we as a team have let ourselves down at times.

"We've failed to hit the sort of mark that, not only we expect of ourselves, but I think that England fans expect of their team.

"But I am also hugely excited. The talent we got in this group hasn't really got a ceiling. Some of the young guys that are coming through and have only got a handful of caps, you can really see being part of this England team for a very, very long time.

"Couple that with the leadership we've got at the top with Maro, Ellis Genge, Jamie George, George Ford and those sorts of figures, and we've got a real good balance in the squad."
