articles.title: New Zealand cruise to victory as Scotland fade at Murrayfield
articles.summary: New Zealand canter to a 43-21 Nations Championship win at Murrayfield as Scotland fall away after a thrilling first half.
articles.body:
Tries: Sititi, De Groot, Taylor, Barrett 2, Moorby, Aumua Cons: McKenzie 4

Ruthless New Zealand blew Scotland away in a high-class, seven tries to three Nations Championship victory at Murrayfield.

Despite a historic first-half hat-trick from Scotland hooker Ewan Ashman, the All Blacks were mostly magnificent, unrelenting and classy. It was the 34th Test between the nations and New Zealand's tally has yet another win - 32 now, with two draws going back to 1905.

Wallace Sititi scored early in a breathless first half. Ashman responded. Ethan de Groot and Codie Taylor hit back to make it 17-7 at the end of the first quarter.

New Zealand's Peter Lakai was binned and Ashman got his second while he was off. The sensational Beauden Barrett scored the first of his double straight after. Then, as the bonkerdom stretched on, Sititi was yellow-carded and Ashman made the All Blacks pay with his hat-trick try.

Only three points divided them at the break, but the All Blacks outclassed Scotland thereafter. Josh Moorby, Beauden Barrett again and Asafo Aumua struck in the second half. Scotland were beaten out the gate in the end.

We hoped for a classic and a classic it was, with bells on. If only for 40 minutes. Beyond that thrilling opening spell it was one-way traffic, a vicious exhibition of All Black class and might.

Just like last year, when New Zealand drew first blood, the visitors came roaring out, punishing a penalty given away cheaply with a piece of trickery at a close-range line-out that bamboozled the Scots. A couple of dummy runners broke away and took enough of Scotland's attention with them. Sititi thundered through a gap to score.

Thus began the ding-dong. Kyle Rowe's magnificent 50-22 gave Scotland the field position to strike off a driven line-out - Ashman driving over for the first of his three tries. Unlike his counterpart, Damian McKenzie, Finn Russell converted. Scotland led by two.

New Zealand turned the screw again, forcing Scotland into big defensive set after big defensive set. There's only so much of that you can soak up, though. The visitors looked lethal from all corners. Beauden Barrett's surge downfield, hotly pursued by Matt Fagerson, was the catalyst for their second score.

Fagerson was done on the floor, New Zealand went to touch and De Groot went over the line. McKenzie converted; New Zealand by five. And, soon, New Zealand by 10. Another Scotland penalty was punished to the max, the All Blacks executing from the resultant line-out maul. Taylor getting it down this time.

This all happened inside the first quarter. On it went. Lakai, the terrific openside, was binned for persistent New Zealand offsides. Huw Jones almost scored but got held up. Scotland came again. Off a penalty advantage, Ashman blasted through Sititi to score. Two for the hooker. With Russell's conversion it was a three-point game.

Scotland needed to kick on, but instead they got pushed back. The wondrous Beauden Barrett sliced through following huge work from his pack; on the face it simple, but in reality, complex and beautiful. McKenzie restored the 10-point lead, but it didn't last long.

Sititi was binned for going off his feet. Scotland had a crack at 13 All Blacks for a brief minute but couldn't break them despite going painfully close through Jones. Lakai returned to make it 15 versus 14 - and that's when Scotland struck.

It was that old reliable again, the line-out maul proving devastating. Ashman got on the end of it and over he went for his hat-trick. For a flurry of penalties and back-to-back yellows, New Zealand got what they deserved. Those cards cost them 14 points.

Seven first-half tries and three points between them at the break. Now it was time for Test match animals to emerge. When they did, they were wearing New Zealand white rather than Scotland blue.

The All Blacks played those key minutes in Scotland's 22, forcing errors and penalties and opportunities. Off a scrum, Jordie Barrett's skip pass found Moorby in space and he sauntered over. Ruthlessness again. McKenzie converted; 29-21. And worrying.

More New Zealand heat and more Scotland penalties. Then, a yellow for Sione Tuipulotu. It could have been Ben White just as easily. The pressure the visitors were applying was just suffocating.

With the captain off the pitch, New Zealand made it pay - Quinn Tupaea to McKenzie and on to Beauden Barrett for his second of the day. Skill-set through the roof.

McKenzie's conversion made it 36-21. At 50 minutes, the game was over far too early for Gregor Townsend's side. To rub salt in the wound Aumua finished a gorgeous set-piece to land try number seven; 43-21 and 19-0 in the second half.

Scotland had hopes of winning or, at the very least, of taking New Zealand to the wire. The uneasy truth for Townsend and his players is that despite their excellence in the opening half, they were utterly bossed in the second.

These All Blacks are far more formidable than the version that appeared at Murrayfield a year ago. Meanwhile, Scotland's long, long wait for glory against the Kiwis carries on and on.

Replacements: Gregor Hiddleston, Pierre Schoeman, Will Hurd, Max Williamson, Josh Baylish, George Horne, Tom Jordan, Blair Kinghorn.

articles.title: Nations Championship schedule, results, kick-off times and how to watch
articles.summary: Everything you need to know as the inaugural edition of the competition continues
articles.body:
Rugby's Nations Championship bursts back into life as the inaugural edition comes to a conclusion in a busy November.

The new competition pits the Six Nations sides against the four Rugby Championship competitors, plus Japan and Fiji, across six matches split evenly across the July and November Test windows.

The results of those games will determine each of the 12 teams' seedings for the finals weekend at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium , with six matches contested over two days and both team and hemisphere silverware up for grabs.

Each entrant will be matched against the equivalent qualifier from the other pool to decide overall placings at the conclusion of a busy year of international action. France and South Africa currently top the two pools, with New Zealand also unbeaten and level on points with the Springboks.

Here's the full competition schedule, and how it will all work:

Announced during the 2023 Rugby World Cup, the new competition will be held every other year and replaces the traditional summer tours and Autumn Nations Series. It is designed to add context to the international calendar, with Fiji and Japan invited to join the Six Nations and Rugby Championship sides to form a top 12. Promotion and relegation is planned for the future with the second-tier Nations Cup, though will not take place in 2026.

Northern Hemisphere : France, Ireland, Scotland, Italy, England, Wales.

Southern Hemisphere: South Africa, New Zealand, Argentina, Australia, Fiji, Japan.

The first finals weekend will be held at Twickenham on the last weekend (27 to 29) of November. Three days of double-headers will be held at the ground, with the first-placed finisher of the Six Nations sides meeting whoever tops the other pool, and so on and so forth down the rankings.

The winner of that marquee match will lift the first Nations Championship trophy, while whichever hemisphere – a term used loosely with Japan included in the "southern" section and Fiji hosting their games in the United Kingdom – wins more final matches will also be crowned. The 1st vs 1st match is worth two points, with all other matches in the finals weekend worth one.

Viewers in the United Kingdom will be able to watch every game on ITV after the free-to-air broadcaster struck a deal to show the competition.

articles.title: El XV del León sabe sufrir y escapa de la derrota ante Uruguay
articles.standfirst: Un ensayo de Minguillón y una defensa sobre la línea salvan el resultado
articles.summary: Un ensayo de Minguillón y una defensa sobre la línea salvan el resultado
articles.body: Pablo Bouza decía antes del partido ante Uruguay, interpelado sobre si el XV del León empezaba a sentir presión, que influía sobre la percepción y la exigencia al equipo el hecho de que España consiguió muy buenos resultados al principio de su ciclo como seleccionador, que por el momento ha llevado el equipo al Mundial. Ahora España no puede presentarse a ningún partido como equipo que aspira a sorprender sino que está ya muy estudiado por todos los rivales y por tanto las dificultades son mayores, así, ayer rondó la derrota ante Uruguay en el inicio de la segunda fase de la World Rugby Nations Cup. Se ganó por 18-12 (ensayos 2-2), pero a pocos minutos de final la ventaja era uruguaya y en un partido en el que el equipo español no lograba imponer su juego. Puede hablarse de que estamos en el inicio de la Ventana y que el equipo aún está madurando, pero el hecho es que el equipo pareció haber retrocedido un tanto desde sus mejores momentos, hace un año. Uruguay consiguió que el partido se jugara en su terreno, un choque muy trabado de delanteras en el que, además, llevaron ventaja porque el equipo español no pudo imponer continuidad en su juego. Hasta el minuto 56 España no pudo ejecutar su mejor arma, el touch-maul, y además los uruguayos defendieron bien la acción. Quizá lo mejor fue el XV del León mantuvo la concentración. Anotó su primer ensayo por medio de Alejandro Laforga en el primer tiempo y aunque en el minuto 68 un posado uruguayo puso el marcador en el 11-12, ya sin jugadores como Bay o Zabala en el campo, el XV del León siguió intentándolo y una acción por fin de tres cuartos generó un oval que acabó llegando a las manos de Gauthier Minguillon, que anotó un ensayo casi definitivo, porque lo realmente decisivo fue una gran acción defensiva de delantera contra delantera, ya con el reloj a cero. No fue el mejor partido, repetimos, pero se salvó el resultado y el XV del León demostró que también puede ganar cuando no tiene el mejor día. Pablo Bouza no acabó contento con el juego de ataque pero sí con el desempeño de los jugadores de refresco. La semana que viene, Chile, otro equipo poderoso el delantera, y con muchos cambios en España. Ficha técnica. 18. España: Futeu, Ovejero, Zabala, Piñeiro, Suárez, Foulds, Ariceta, Nieto; Bay, Güemes; Laforga, Fernández, Mateu, Cian y Bell. También jugaron Santamaría, Vélez, Marsinyac, Pirlet, Aurrekoetxea, Boronat, Diego González y Minguillon. 12. Uruguay: Sanguinetti, Kessler, Piussi, Dotti, Leindekar, Arado, Bianchi, Diana; Rodríguez Bosch, Amarillo; Facciolo, Suárez, Ferrario, Juan González e Ignacio Álvarez. También jugaron Aliaga, Vidal, Sebas Pérez y Peculo, Marcador: 3-0, min.9: golpe de Mateu. 3-7, min.11: ensayo de Ferrario, que pasa Amarillo. 8-7, min.23, ensayo de Laforga. 11-7, min.54: golpe de Mateu. 11-12, min.69: ensayo de Ferrario. 18-12, min.73: ensayo de Minguillon, que pasa Mateu. Árbitro: Ben O´Keeffe, de Nueva Zelanda. Incidencias: Partido correspondiente a la cuarta jornada de la Copa de las Naciones disputado en el Estadio Nacional de la Universidad Complutense de Madrid. Se formaron largas colas a la entrada del estadio.

articles.title: Nations Championship - England 45-22 Australia: Henry Pollock stars out of position on the wing in morale-boosting Twickenham victory
articles.summary: Jamie George, Ollie Chessum, Joe Heyes, Jack van Poortvliet, Henry Pollock (two) and Ben Spencer score as England ease pressure on Steve Borthwick with bonus-point win over Australia; Pollock played second half on the wing, replacing injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso
articles.body:
In a week when Borthwick came under intense scrutiny following newspaper reports of a summer rift with his England squad - claims denied by Jamie George to Sky Sports - England responded with a seven-try performance and record point haul against Australia.

Hooker George, back-row Ollie Chessum, tighthead Joe Heyes and scrum-half Jack van Poortvliet all crossed, while replacements Henry Pollock (twice) and Ben Spencer also got on the scoresheet.

Pollock, ordinarily a back-row forward, replaced the stricken Immanuel Feyi-Waboso (ankle) at half-time, featuring on the wing for 40 minutes and hardly looking out of place.

Fin Smith added five conversions and ran England's attack well from fly-half, while Australia scored via wings Max Jorgensen and Filipo Daugunu, and back-row Jeremy Williams, but struggled for parity in terms of the power stakes.

The Wallabies also suffered a costly blow when loosehead prop Angus Bell was sin-binned in the first half, becoming the first player penalised for a hip-drop tackle since World Rugby outlawed it this month.

England looked to have scored less than two minutes in when Feyi-Waboso scorched through, but the TMO soon showed replays of a forward pass from Ben Curry to Chessum earlier in the move to chalk off the score.

England kept up their early intensity, producing a choke-tackle maul turnover and attacking off the consequent midfield scrum with Feyi-Waboso central again, but that good work was undone by lock Alex Coles when he flew off his feet at a breakdown in the Wallabies' 22 to give away a penalty.

The hosts were soon back into the 22 when Australia coughed up a soft obstruction penalty under a high ball - Smith producing a fine kick into the corner - and from the subsequent maul, George was on hand to touch down.

Smith hit the post with the conversion, and soon Australia were onto the scoreboard via the boot of Ryan Lonergan, who split the uprights with a penalty after the England backline were caught offside off a lineout.

Superb work from Maro Itoje in the Australia 22 to charge down Lonergan then forced a knock-on, earning England a scrum to attack off within the Australia 22, but Heyes was penalised for an early push to see the chance blown.

Errors continued to flow from the hosts as Feyi-Waboso spilled possession on the run in the 22, George was pinged for crooked throw and a scrum penalty was shipped too.

Mistakes then proved contagious when Australia hooker Billy Pollard was pinged for a crooked throw himself in the England half, rendering the contest firmly top-start.

Feyi-Waboso soon displayed his pace and dynamism again at the end of a nice backline move, but England lost the ball again in the 22.

Yet, Australia just couldn't handle Feyi-Waboso and the pressure finally told as the wing made a burst down the opposite wing, and once England chipped the ball wide, Chessum was too powerful for Jorgensen to score.

Smith converted well for a 12-3 lead, before Itoje executed a strip for another chance - despite a couple of forward passes being missed - but a George Furbank neck-roll in the 22 saw the Wallabies clear.

Australia were then reduced to 14, however, as the TMO showed images of a Bell hip-drop tackle on Feyi-Waboso.

Henry Slade kicked to corner, and the maul did the trick again as Heyes wrestled the ball out and dived over for England's third of the half.

Two minutes before half-time, Tommy Freeman should have scored England's fourth but knocked on a bouncing ball in-goal after winning the chase.

Instead, the visitors notched a try out of nothing in the final minute before half-time; Jorgenson intercepting a telegraphed Van Poortvliet pass near halfway and showing his pace to sprint over.

That left the half-time deficit a nine-point one, but just before Bell was due to re-emerge from his sin-bin period, England scored their fourth three minutes into the second half: Pollock carrying brilliantly down the left to start things, and Freeman doing fabulous work down the right before finding Van Poorvliet with a long pass.

Australia threatened a try back in response when centre Isaac Henry cut through England and broke to near the 22, but the Wallabies were pinged for sealing off.

Henry then made a big error in skewing a kick out on the full as the Wallabies sought to attack from deep, and England did not let up until they had a fifth try as Pollock finished out wide after Australia had been pushed back in tight carries near the try-line.

Within two minutes, Pollock was celebrating again, as another rapid backline attack well-orchestrated by Smith saw the makeshift wing finish with swagger down the right.

Past the hour mark, the Wallabies did score again as Daugunu finished a flowing move in the left corner, but it went unconverted when Lonergan couldn't land the tough kick.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii passed up a certain try when he shipped the ball to Jorgensen instead of finishing, but Australia scored from the resulting England lineout in any case - the hosts sloppy near their own try-line and Williams finishing.

England soon forgot about that mistake, though, as Spencer intercepted a Daugunu offload to race into the corner and round off a big victory.

Pollock: Coaches wouldn't put me on wing if they didn't think I could do it

"The biggest thing is the rugby stuff. Pleasure and privilege. For me, the biggest thing is going out there and showcasing myself and the growth of this team throughout the summer and into the autumn.

"I love playing for this team, I love playing back at home. We spoke about being back at home and creating some energy around that.

"The coaches wouldn't put me on the wing if they knew I couldn't do anything there, so the big thing for me is going out there and being as confident as I can.

"If I mess up, I'm playing a new position, I'm going to make some new learnings from it. If there's any young kids out there, playing new positions, just take each step as it comes.

"I made a few mistakes today, but the boys outside me, like Slade in the corner, backed me up. That just made my job so much easier.

"I disagree with that [versatility potentially working agasint him], versatility is a massive thing. Today, my role was coming on in the second half and being a winger. I trust the coaches and the team, whatever they need to do for that.

"It showed in that last 30-40 minutes, the bench came on and did their thing. That shows where we're at as a squad."

George 'proud' of team-mates after tough week

"I wonder where that's come from? [big try celebration]

"It's [newspaper reports] been a distraction. I'm so unbelievably proud of how the team looked after each other, stepped up for each other, and we are a tight team regardless.

"As I said, it probably brought us even tighter and being back at Allianz Stadium is just unbelievable."

England captain Maro Itoje said to ITV Sport:

"I am over the moon. This week has been great, great for me personally to be back in camp.

"I think we're starting to show what we can do, we've got a very talented team, and it's now time for us to put it all together.

"Sometimes when you have time away from the team, as I did in the summer, it makes you appreciate what playing for England is all about.

"When I stood out there for the National Anthems, it gave me goosebumps. These are the games I want to be a part of."

Wilson: We can't be waiting until last 15 minutes to start playing

Australia captain Harry Wilson told ITV Sport:

"England put us under the pump, we didn't get too much ball in the first-half. We didn't get too many A-zone entries and England were the better team today.

"They fronted up physically, put us under the pump. Our defence wasn't physical enough in slowing the ball down.

"I feel like we were playing from behind there, so, credit to England.

"A lot of our issues might be mindset. We've got seven days to take some feedback from this game and make sure we're a lot better.

"I know Scotland are a really good team, and we have to be ready for it, and we have to be ready for these harsh lessons.

"We know when we hold the ball for long phases and play our style of footy, we can cut teams up. But we can't be waiting for the last 15 minutes to do it."

For England, they next face Japan in their second Nations Championship Test of the autumn at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Saturday November 14 (4.40pm kick-off).

Australia travel to face Scotland at Murrayfield for their next Test, on Sunday November 15 (3.10pm kick-off).

articles.title: Nations Championship: Sione Tuipulotu takes 'full responsibility' for Scotland collapse
articles.summary: Captain Sione Tuipulotu takes responsibility for Scotland's second-half Nations Championship collapse against New Zealand, saying they were "nowhere near accurate enough".
articles.body:
Captain Sione Tuipulotu took responsibility for Scotland's second-half Nations Championship collapse against New Zealand, saying they were "nowhere near accurate enough".

Trailing by just three points at half-time, Scotland were well in the contest as they sought a first victory against the All Blacks at the 34th attempt.

However, they failed to score any points in the second half as New Zealand swept to a clinical 43-21 victory at Murrayfield.

Tuipulotu was sin-binned on 50 minutes after a succession of penalties went against the Scots and they were unable to wrestle back momentum from there.

"Disappointing," was Tuipulotu's one-word review post-match.

He added: "We played our rugby in the first half but we probably left points out there. We were nowhere near accurate enough second half, and we couldn't stick with them, it's really disappointing.

"Our discipline wasn't good enough, and it starts with me. I got sent to the bin and 10 minutes with your captain off isn't good for any team. I take full responsibility for that."

Scotland's familiar frailties brutally exposed in All Blacks schooling

New Zealand cruise to victory as Scotland fade

All the Scottish rugby latest in one place

Scotland conceded 13 penalties to New Zealand's eight. Just moments after Tuipulotu went to the bin, Beauden Barrett cruised over to score his second and New Zealand's sixth try of the day. Game over.

"First half we were playing our rugby, putting them under pressure with ball in hand, in a way they haven't been put under pressure over the past couple of weeks," Tuipulotu said.

"We just weren't accurate enough when we got down into the 22m. We had lots of opportunities in the first half and weren't accurate enough in the second.

"We know what we can do with ball in hand, which proves we weren't up to the level that the All Blacks were playing in the second half.

"It's a must-win game [against Australia] next week, we'll regroup and stick together like we always do."

In the first half, Scotland's maul and New Zealand's indiscipline kept the hosts in touch. After the interval, the All Blacks tightened up defensively and scored three magnificent tries.

"Scotland kept getting the wrong side of Andrew Brace with Sione Tuiputotu going to the sin-bin," former Scotland captain John Barclay said on STV.

"But the difference is red zone efficiency - when the team gets into the opposition 22m, how often do they score? New Zealand were at 58%, Scotland were at 30%.

"There's a couple moments in the second half where they manage to get down into the 22m, and they lost the ball first phase. It's that clinical edge."

There has long been a perception this Scotland team have the ability to beat anyone on their day, but that they fail to deliver 80-minute performances.

This was a classic of the genre and head coach Gregor Townsend says there is plenty of work to be done.

"We gave them too many opportunities with our discipline," Townsend said, echoing the verdict of his captain.

"The second half, we never got to build on the good work from the first half - largely, because we didn't have the ball. Sometimes we made errors, and then with the yellow card we were having to defend for a lot of that period.

"It was disappointing. Whenever I see this team prepare, I feel we've got a chance to beat anyone. I felt that today, and I felt it at half-time, but it didn't happen.

"Both sides of the ball, we've got to be harder to be broken down. Our defence was actually doing well. At times we were driving New Zealand back. But whether it was an offside, or an error around the breakdown, we were getting penalised and put into our 22m."

Scotland's Six Nations wins over Wales and England were followed by a shock defeat by Italy. They responded by beating France in a stunning display before finishing their campaign by losing against Ireland.

Last autumn, a narrower scoreline against New Zealand came just before a spectacular collapse against Argentina. They entertain and infuriate in equal measure.

Townsend's side welcome Australia and Japan to Murrayfield this month as they attempt to end their Nations Championship campaign on a high.

"I still feel the players we have and the way we set up to play, we should cause opposition problems," Townsend said.

"New Zealand had the nudge in the scrum at times, and they were very good around the ruck, so credit to them. They deserved the win, clearly.

"We're going to learn from it. It was a lesson on making sure our error rate and our discipline needs to be much better. If you give so many turnovers and penalties away to a good team like New Zealand, you're not going to win."

articles.title: Wales 28-21 Japan: Steve Tandy's side labour to Nations Championship win
articles.summary: Wales resumed their Nations Championship campaign with an unconvincing bonus-point 28-21 victory against Japan at the Principality Stadium.
articles.body:
Tries: Griffin, Adams 2, Rees-Zammit Cons: Costelow 3, Edwards

Tries: Gunter, Dearns, Fukuda, Cons: Saito 2, Komura

Wales resumed their Nations Championship campaign with an unconvincing bonus-point victory against Japan at the Principality Stadium.

Tries from prop Archie Griffin, wing Josh Adams and the rejuvenated Louis Rees-Zammit gave Wales a 21-14 half-time lead, with Japan responding with scores from flanker Ben Gunter and lock Warner Dearns.

In a nervy second half, Adams scored his second try before Japan replacement Kenta Fukuda ensured the visitors finished with a losing bonus point and presented a frantic finale which the hosts survived.

Wales secured a fourth win for head coach Steve Tandy in 13 internationals and provided another narrow victory against Eddie Jones' Japan to mirror the last-gasp Jarrod Evans penalty that sealed a one-point win 12 months ago.

Wales were indebted to strong ball-carrying performances from player-of-the-match Rees-Zammit, full-back Blair Murray, back-row duo Morgan and Wainwright and centre Eddie James.

Tandy should be very concerned about their malfunctioning line-out with six lost, the way they allowed Japan to stay in the game, worrying indiscipline, and wasting attacking opportunities with silly handling errors.

Nations Championship: Wales edge Japan but underwhelm - reaction

New Zealand cruise to victory as Scotland fade

Wales stay in fifth place in the northern hemisphere table after returning to the inaugural international competition.

They had started the tournament in July with a home win over Fiji and defeats in Argentina and South Africa, while Japan had defeated Italy but lost to Ireland and France.

The game was played in front of 52,425 supporters, which was 2,000 more than the opening match against Argentina last November but 9,000 down on the attendance that watched the match against Japan in Cardiff in 2025.

Wales host New Zealand next Saturday before finishing the regular league campaign against Australia, while Japan will travel to face England and Scotland.

Allianz Stadium in Twickenham will then host a three-day finals weekend at the end of November. If the tables stay the same, Wales will play Japan again for the fifth-placed finish in south-west London.

Familiar foes return for another Cardiff date

Wales and Japan have been frequent opponents in recent times, with this representing the fourth meeting between the two nations in 16 months.

Tandy named a record nine English-based club players in his starting side, including six of the pack, with 12 of the 23-strong squad based outside of Wales, with seven alterations from the 43-0 defeat to South Africa in July.

With Ryunosuke Ito unavailable because of his university commitments in Japan, Jones handed a debut to third-choice fly-half Riku Kitahara as part of a half-back pairing with co-captain Naoto Saito.

Rees-Zammit, who has moved back to his favoured wing position after filling in at full-back, lifted the crowd with a searing early break.

It laid the foundations for Lake to power towards the line before prop Griffin, who had not trained on Friday, flopped over for his first Test try, which Sam Costelow converted.

Careless Wales play allowed Japan to steal possession from a home breakdown as scrum-half Tomos Williams was caught, with flanker Gunter outflanking Josh Adams and Alex Mann. Saito converted.

Wales responded with a Wainwright break into the Japan 22, but they again failed to protect possession at the breakdown.

Wales were fielding one of their biggest ever centre combinations in James, 6ft 4in (1.90m) and 16st 3lbs (103kg), and Max Llewellyn, 6ft 6in (1.96m) and 16st 12lbs (107kg).

The pair had not started together at Test level before, as Tandy named his sixth different centre combination in his 13th international.

James had two early bursts down the left-hand side but another knock-on, which was a fifth handling error in 15 minutes, demonstrated the inaccuracy of the opening quarter.

Wales produced a pedestrian attacking period that included Costelow being tackled heavily twice, before Ben Carter was penalised for a neck roll.

Wales showed a more clinical nature as they regained the lead when Adams crossed after prominent build-up work from James, Morgan and Rees-Zammit.

The hosts again let the opposition back into the game because of poor discipline, and Dearns capitalised by diving over as Japan once more levelled the scores.

Wales' line-out issues continued when an attacking set-piece play five metres from Japan's line was thwarted by a not-straight Lake throw.

The home side were able to strike just before half-time with Rees-Zammit starting and finishing the move for his first try in eight internationals.

Rees-Zammit was helped by an eye-catching power burst through a Saito tackle and offload from the impressive James.

The home side were again guilty of conceding possession from the restart, but prop Nicky Smith produced an important turnover on his own line to help Wales lead by seven points at half-time.

Wales had an early second-half chance to score following a well-worked try as Costelow inexplicably kicked possession away with Murray and Rees-Zammit outside him.

The home side also lost another attacking line-out in the Japan 22, while Wales were guilty of conceding more lazy penalties.

Tandy's side were indebted to a Lake turnover penalty, which was the hooker's final contribution as the front row was replaced.

Wainwright and Morgan again powered through the Japan defence but the attacking move again ended with another speculative Costelow cross-kick that Rees-Zammit was unable to gather.

Wales continued to prove wasteful in their attacking endeavours while the line-out misfired.

The home fans were relieved when the bonus-point try essentially sealed the victory, with Murray counter-attacking before feeding scrum-half Tomos Williams, with Adams finishing off the move.

Japan were not finished, and a flowing move was finished by replacement scrum-half Fukuda to bring the visitors to within seven points.

Adams calmed the nerves with a turnover penalty as Wales held on.

When Wales analyse this underwhelming display, Tandy will know they have to improve dramatically before the All Blacks arrive next weekend.

Wales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, James, Llewellyn, Adams; Costelow, Tomos Williams; Smith, Lake (capt), Griffin, Jenkins, Carter, Mann, Morgan, Wainwright.

Replacements: Elias, Carre, Francis, Teddy Williams, Botham, Morgan-Williams, D Edwards, Hennessey.

Japan: Ueda; Ishida, Riley, Tua, Burua; Kitahara, Saito (co-capt); Kamimori, Harada, Takeuchi, Hockings, Dearns (co-capt), Gunter, Shimokawa, Cornelsen.

articles.title: Scotland's familiar frailties brutally exposed in All Blacks schooling
articles.summary: Hopes of a first-ever win over New Zealand were trampled along with Scotland's mission statement, writes Tom English.
articles.body:
Fair play to the All Blacks. At least this time they didn't wait until the closing minutes to put Scotland away, they took them out of their misery way earlier than that. A small mercy, in a sense.

No dramas, no late moments of All Black genius required, no clutch try to swing it in the end and break Scottish hearts. Those late sucker-punches? They're the worst.

It's easier this way. You know where you are with shellackings. It's the near misses that are harder to take.

If you're going to lose to the All Blacks, maybe it's better to be routed than robbed, better to be outclassed than walking away with a sense of grievance or a feeling a win was left behind.

This was a systematic dismantling, all over in the 51st minute when Beauden Barrett, as much of a genius now at the age of 35 as he ever was, scored his second try of the day.

Barrett is now on 50 Test tries and 148 caps. Murrayfield witnessed one of the all-time greats on Saturday; classy, intelligent and ruthless. Any notion Scotland could bring an end to 121 years without a win against New Zealand was trampled underfoot by Barrett and his band of brothers; blood brothers and otherwise.

Tuipulotu takes 'full responsibility' for Scotland collapse

New Zealand cruise to victory as Scotland fade

The first half was a thrill-fest, the second half was an annihilation. At the break, with Ewan Ashman having completed his hat-trick and Murrayfield rocking, the great Richie McCaw stood away to the side, just below the media gantry.

Was he ashen-faced - or Ashman-faced - at the space Scotland were finding and the tries they were scoring? Was he fretful this just might be the day the record tumbles?

Er, no. He took out his phone and started tapping in the manner of a guy ordering a taxi - for Scotland, of course. McCaw, and every All Black in his wake, don't worry in moments like this.

They just up the ante and back themselves. They increase the intensity, the accuracy, the power. They feast on mistakes and accelerate away.

The second half was 19-0 to the All Blacks. That's what outstanding rugby teams do. Away from home against a dangerous team in front of a loud crowd. They embrace adversity. They get turned on by it.

Dave Rennie's favourite word, in a rugby context, is brutal, as in brutal physicality, brutal execution, brutal in putting a foot on an opponent's throat and keeping it there. All of that was visited upon Scotland. New Zealand were better and smarter. Their rugby IQ was on a different level.

Gregor Townsend and his players spoke later about where it all went wrong. Didn't take enough of their chances in the first half, didn't make it hard enough for New Zealand to get field position, didn't survive at the breakdown, didn't deliver on discipline, didn't look after ball.

All true, but the greater truth is that after three close Tests under Townsend since 2017, New Zealand have now pulled miles clear of Scotland.

Townsend can talk about all the little things and some of the big things Scotland got wrong but these things didn't suddenly afflict his team. They didn't just drop out of the sky. They're in the DNA of this team. We have seen these failings before in defeat and even in victory.

Scotland's attack can be a thing of wonder, capable of creating space and delivering sensational tries against the very best teams on the planet. They did it on Saturday against the All Blacks, they did it against South Africa in July, they did it against France and Ireland in March. These are good rugby players.

The elite teams pride themselves on defence - and that's where Scotland are mired in quicksand. They conceded five tries in defeat to the Pumas last autumn. In victory, they put 50 on France but conceded 40 points and six tries.

They shipped 43 points against Ireland and another six tries. They lost 42-18 to the Boks in the summer and gave up another six tries. They beat the Pumas but, again, their inability to be savage on the other side of the ball saw them conceding 38 points and five tries. It was another 40-pointer against the All Blacks - and another six tries.

Townsend must repair morale as Wallabies await

There were lovely moments in all of those Tests, but Scotland's big mantra coming into the autumn was all about making life difficult for opponents, making sure every yard they made in possession was only won after a battle, every try they scored was only achieved after fighting for their lives through the phases.

Worthy sentiments and an important mission statement, but four minutes into it on Saturday, New Zealand threw a bit of trickery at Scotland at a lineout and scored with ease.

The piece of deception - two runners bolting off a lineout as decoy men - has been done by a few teams already this season. It wasn't a revelation but it was enough to fool Scotland.

The irony came in the name of the scorer. Scotland wanted their defence to be Braveheart in its, well, brutality. Wallace Sititi scored that first try. The back-row was named after William Wallace. So much for freedom from concession of soft scores.

The All Blacks got to 43 points with 12 minutes left. They could have had more, but they'd made their point. They're back. Not at Springbok level, clearly, but improving.

Rennie, and his sidekick Mike Blair, have brought huge improvement in a relatively short time. These All Blacks are light years ahead of the version Scott Robertson brought here 12 months ago.

Townsend must now piece together shattered morale and go again next Sunday. The Wallabies are up next. Scotland have won four of their past five against Australia, all under Townsend, and will be expected to make it five from six.

The Wallabies will fancy a crack at them, though. They'll respect Scotland's ability with ball in hand but relish a shot at exposing the weakness in their ranks. You don't need 20-20 vision to spot the frailties in this team. The All Blacks found them with ease in that sobering second-half schooling.

articles.title: Dewi Lake says Wales let themselves down in Japan win
articles.summary: Captain Dewi Lake knows there is plenty to improve following a lacklustre 28-21 Nations Championship victory over Japan.
articles.body:
Captain Dewi Lake says Wales let themselves down during the lacklustre 28-21 Nations Championship victory against Japan in Cardiff.

Josh Adams added two tries to scores from prop Archie Griffin and wing Louis Rees-Zammit as Wales claimed a bonus-point win.

This was their second victory from four games in the competition but Lake was left frustrated with aspects of the performance.

"There were massive parts of that game where we let ourselves down," he said.

"Getting into camp, we said we were going to do things that we probably didn't do against Japan.

"That's disappointing but this is a group that wants to grow and will challenge each other."

Nations Championship: Wales edge Japan but underwhelm - reaction

Wales labour to bonus-point win against Japan

In front of a crowd of 52,425 supporters, Wales had to hold on for only the fourth win in Steve Tandy's 13 Tests in charge, two of which have come against Japan.

Lake said a victory should not be underestimated with Wales having suffered recent losing streaks, which included a record 18 consecutive Test defeats in a row.

"A win is massive for this group, for the confidence and trust we'll get in each other," he said.

"We were happy with the win and it's something we've not done often enough, so I am proud of the boys."

Wales remain fifth in the northern hemisphere table but face much tougher challenges this month.

New Zealand, fresh from defeating Scotland, are the visitors to Cardiff next Saturday before Australia play at the Principality Stadium on 21 November.

"If you look at the two Test matches, we did things today that weren't good enough to compete in those games," said Lake.

"We'll have to get a lot right next week and fix some stuff."

Head coach Tandy said he was expecting more from his side this weekend.

"It's good to start the campaign with a bonus-point win but I can't run away from the performance when I talk about it," said Tandy.

"There are elements of the performance we definitely need to improve. I thought we'd be better than that in some elements.

"There was good stuff from us, in terms of the line breaks and how we opened Japan up, but we weren't ruthless enough.

"We'll definitely have to do that for the next couple of games but it helps to review after a win."

Japan head coach Eddie Jones said it was an opportunity missed to win a first game in Cardiff against Wales.

"That could have been a historic win for us but you've got to be good enough to take advantage of those mistakes," he said.

"We weren't quite good enough and it was certainly a missed opportunity."

Jones said he was proud of his young team but believes they needed to be more clinical.

"If you watch rugby now, once you get in the 22 and if you don't take points from that, that's the difference in the game," said Jones.

"We had three opportunities but we didn't take chances and Wales did. Their points-per-entry was higher than ours."

Jones questioned some aspects of the interpretation of New Zealand referee Paul Williams at the contact area.

"I hope I'm not going to get in trouble for this but there was one penalty for not supporting your weight at the breakdown and it was against us," said Jones.

"Anyone watching that game, can you think there was just one ruck where the supporting player was off his feet?

"That can be the difference between winning and losing.

"I'm not complaining, I'm just saying sometimes you don't get the rub of the green.

"That can happen. You've got to suck it up and get on with it. Actually maybe I am complaining!"

Japan travel to face Jones' former England side at Allianz Stadium at Twickenham next Saturday.

articles.title: 2026 Women's Rugby League World Cup: Australia reach final after Fiji scare
articles.summary: Australia have reached their fifth successive Women's Rugby League World Cup final as they seek a fourth consecutive title - but they were made to work harder than anyone expected.
articles.body:
Tries: Church 4, Upton, Chapman Goals: Kelleher 3

Tries: Yaranamua, Paseka Goals: Yaranamua 3

Australia have reached their fifth successive Women's Rugby League World Cup final as they seek a fourth consecutive title - but they were made to work harder than anyone expected.

They had breezed through the group stages and there looked to be little to stop the procession.

But World Cup debutants Fiji had other ideas. For 40 minutes, one of the biggest surprises in the history of rugby league looked eminently possible.

Order was eventually restored, thanks largely to four tries from Abbi Church, which set Australia on their way to a 30-14 victory.

They will face old rivals New Zealand in the final next Sunday in Brisbane, kicking off at 05:10 GMT.

But having given New Zealand a scare in their opening match before losing 18-12, Fiji came out at Sydney Football Stadium fully intent to unsettle and confront the red-hot tournament favourites.

In doing so, they became the first side since New Zealand in the 2013 World Cup final to open the scoring in a game against Australia, who trailed for the first time at this tournament.

Church scores four as Australia beat Fiji to reach Women's RL World Cup final - as it happened

The tournament debutants put pressure on the Australia line from the start. Soon the entire Aussie team caught the bug with simple drops and brainless errors, and after 12 minutes Simaima Taufa conceded a penalty under the posts.

Fiji opted to kick for two points. Four minutes later, they went all the way.

Captain Sereana Naitokatoka stole the ball from Jaime Chapman 10 metres from the Australia line, and they drove through the defence for half-back Luisa Yaranamua to score. She also converted to give Fiji an astonishing 8-0 lead.

At last Australia sparked into life, and two tries in the final 10 minutes of the opening half brought them level.

Church drove over in the right corner, before Tamika Upton slipped through the defence as Australia returned pressure following a Fiji drop-out.

But Jocelyn Kelleher missed twice from the tee to allow Fiji in at half-time level. Had Upton not brilliantly tipped a Fiji grubber behind, Australia would have trailed.

Whatever coach Jess Skinner said in the changing room woke Australia up, and they took control.

Church completed her treble - the third a brilliant catch from a booming Tarryn Aiken kick to the corner and before grounding the ball at full tilt - either side of Chapman diving over.

Normal service resumed. But at last, the Jillaroos have been proved fallible - with a late Maria Paseka try providing a deserved flourish for fearless Fiji.

Church, though, had the last word for Australia - collecting Losana Lutu's kick around 30 metres from her own line before racing clear to score.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Why Wales have a lot to prove despite Japan win
articles.summary: BBC Sport Wales analyses what went right and wrong for Wales in their uninspiring 28-21 win against Japan.
articles.body:
Wales rugby wins have been in short supply in recent years.

So you would think victory in the opening match of a new campaign might be welcomed. Maybe even celebrated.

But the 28-21 win against Japan in the Nations Championship was unconvincing, underwhelming and a nervy struggle.

Head coach Steve Tandy admitted he expected better and captain Dewi Lake stated his team had let themselves down at times against Eddie Jones’ Japan.

It might have been a fourth victory in 13 internationals for Tandy, but the patchy performance left a lot to be desired.

There are much tougher tests to come with New Zealand the visitors in Cardiff next Saturday and Australia in the Welsh capital the following weekend.

BBC Sport Wales analyses what went right and wrong for Wales as the Nations Championship resumed.

Nations Championship: Wales edge Japan but underwhelm - reaction

The shining light was wing Louis Rees-Zammit, who produced a stellar player-of-the-match display.

He set out his stall early on with an incisive break to lift the crowd and later scored his first try in eight internationals.

It was Rees-Zammit‘s most influential international display since his return to rugby from his brief foray with American football and the NFL.

The Bristol star had dabbled with a move to full-back last season, but is now back in his preferred wing position where he can cause the most havoc.

"There aren’t many athletes that can come back from a different sport and get back to playing international rugby like he did so quickly,” said Tandy.

"By his own admission, Zam wants more. He wants to be one of the best wings in the world, if not the best.

"He's got all the attributes to do that, and he's kicked on.”

When the hosts were struggling to break down the Japan defence, Rees-Zammit popped up with powerful bursts, producing five of Wales' 16 line-breaks, making 121 metres and beating 13 defenders.

“The best teams in the world have people that can break the game up, do something out of nothing,” said Tandy.

"He gone up a level and he deserved his man-of-the-match performance."

Wales fans were looking for a statement performance against Japan. A marker to put down as the World Cup looms in under a year.

They were not provided with that but did witness a victory, however scratchy.

So Wales woke up on a Sunday morning with a Test victory to mark. That has not happened often in recent times.

Some of these Wales players will still remember the record-breaking 18-Test losing sequence between 2023 and 2025. If Wales players can take any positives this weekend, it will be victory.

As Tandy said afterwards, it is always easier to debrief a bonus-point victory.

Among the disjointed team performance, there were notable impressive individual displays from the usual suspects.

Back-row duo Aaron Wainwright and Jac Morgan excelled in attack and defence, full-back Blair Murray was a constant attacking threat and wing Josh Adams popped up with two tries.

Centre Eddie James showed glimpses of his power game in a new-look midfield partnership with Max Llewellyn.

While the centre combination did not set the world alight, it warrants further opportunites.

Tandy will not be content with Wales spending long periods defending and only having 40% in territory and possession.

This was emphasised in the tackle count as the hosts made 227 compared to Japan's 115, with Wales finishing with the top eight tacklers in the game.

He will be encouraged by the resolve with Morgan topping the official Nations Championship charts with 24, followed by lock Dafydd Jenkins (23) and Wainwright (20).

Wales also forced 10 turnovers with Alex Mann gaining three, while there were crucial interventions from Lake, Adams and prop Nicky Smith when Japan seemed destined to score.

The most obvious deficiency was the malfunctioning line-out with six throws going astray.

Hookers, Lake and Ryan Elias, struggled to find their jumpers as the Japan man mountain locks of Harry Hockings and co-captain Warner Dearns caused chaos.

Wales coughed up possession, but the line-out failures also disrupted the home side’s attacking maul, which has become the most potent offensive threat in recent time.

“When we did get it right, we got joy from that area, but we would have loved to go to our driving maul more often.

“You have to credit Japan in that area for the defensive work they do.

"They're number one in the world for a reason in this department, but we're always going to look at ourselves first.”

Wales have been notoriously slow starters to new campaigns with Tandy’s team suffering heavy defeats by Argentina 12 months ago and England during the Six Nations in February.

This weekend has proved no exception against a side, like the southern hemisphere outfits, who are battle hardened.

“It's great for us to get a game,” said Tandy.

"It does get clunky in your first hit out since the summer.

"It takes time to build that cohesion back, whereas you look at the amount of games South Africa, New Zealand and Japan have played since the last time we did in July.

"If you look at last year's Six Nations, we got better in every game and we will look to do that again."

After threatening to take control, Wales continually let Japan back into the game as they were guilty of poor handling errors, bouts of indiscipline and lapses in concentration.

“There were moments where we'd go seven points up and there'd be a sloppy knock-on or we'd look for the pass from a line break rather than take the tackle,” said Tandy.

“There are bits where there's lots to like, but in Test matches, you need to be ruthless and reward yourself when on top.”

Wales fly-half Sam Costelow also had a mixed evening as he was guilty of kicking attacking ball away when the home side seemed set to break down the Japan defence.

Neither Costelow or Dan Edwards have nailed down the famous Wales number 10 jersey. The debate about who should fill the shirt will continue.

Wales remain 10th in the world with this victory again coming against a nation ranked between ninth and 12th.

Tandy’s quartet of international successes have been a Japan double and wins in Cardiff against Italy and Fiji.

There was nothing in this most recent performance to suggest Wales are any closer to hauling themselves out of this mini group of nations and ready to break into the world’s top eight.

Tandy is now in his fourth campaign and has yet to demonstrate he can bridge that gap.

New Zealand are next in Cardiff as the All Blacks opened their campaign with an impressive victory against Scotland , that cemented their place as the world's second best side behind South Africa.

Wales have not beaten the All Blacks since 1953. Events of the past weekend suggest that 73-year losing streak will continue, unless there is a dramatic improvement from the home side and New Zealand’s standards drop markedly.

"It is a massive privilege to take on the All Blacks in our stadium," said Tandy.

"We want to test ourselves against the best so this is another awesome opportunity to go play against one of the top two teams in the world.”

How many fans will turn up to watch Wales and All Blacks?

How many fans will come out and watch next Saturday‘s afternoon spectacle will be fascinating after the Japan game was played in front of 52,425 supporters.

How that attendance figure is judged depends on the narrative people choose to adopt.

Some would point to the crowd being 2,000 more than the opening match against Argentina last November and that it was a larger gathering that Ireland attracted to watch them defeat the Pumas in Dublin on Friday night.

Others would note that it was 9,000 down on the attendance that watched Wales win against Japan in Cardiff in November 2025, pointing to the swathes of empty seats, especially in the top tier of a ground which can host more than 72,000.

Those people say it provides further evidence fans are voting with their feet in protest against the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU), because of the continued turmoil within the domestic game.

There will be another comparable figure to judge next weekend because Wales played New Zealand 12 months ago in a 52-26 loss which was witnessed by 68,388.

Whether the Japan win persuades a few more fans to turn up next weekend remains to be seen.

articles.title: Reece Walsh: World Cup semi-final brings out best and worst of Australia star
articles.summary: On a fractious night in Sydney that ended with Australia reaching yet another Men's Rugby League World Cup final, it was no surprise to see Reece Walsh centre stage – for better or worse.
articles.body:
On a fractious night in Sydney, it was no surprise to see Reece Walsh at the centre of the action – for better or worse.

The full-back scored three of Australia's eight tries as they beat Samoa 44-12 to reach a 16th successive men's Rugby League World Cup final.

His two second-half tries helped keep a burgeoning Samoa comeback at bay, while his first-half effort demonstrated his skill and showmanship.

On 32 minutes, Walsh administered the harshest of punishments on Samoa for the smallest amount of defensive laxity, racing through the tiniest gap on the left to score.

In front of approximately 40,000 spectators, the Kangaroos' number one celebrated with a backflip.

It was the kind of celebration you expect from a man once christened by Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V'landys as "the Justin Bieber of rugby league" and "charisma on steroids".

But while thrilling the fans, it gives kittens to those in charge. Walsh lost his boot during the flip; when sitting down to put it back on, TV commentators fretted he had injured himself.

Australia coach Kevin Walters pointedly said there would be no backflips in the second half during a half-time interview – and indeed Walsh reined himself in.

"That's just Reece," Walters told the post-match media conference. "He always brings up something you don't expect.

"The backflip was no different. Impressive though. He did it for some sick kids. They all asked him to do a backflip if he scored a try, so you can't really be against that when he's putting a smile on kids' faces."

More concerning for Walters will be the mistakes Walsh made as he got swept up in the feverish atmosphere.

Two minutes before Walsh's first try, Samoa's Stephen Crichton appeared to have grounded to close the score to 16-6 after Francis Manuleleua had beaten the Aussie full-back to a high ball.

A slow-motion replay led to the debatable conclusion Manuleleua had knocked on. Whether the correct call or not, it was a massive let-off for Walsh.

Samoa began to lose their heads soon after, with a major flashpoint coming after Walsh was ruled to have been dangerously tackled. It was Walsh himself who instigated the ruck after the incident.

Walsh quickly responded after both Samoan scores, keeping them at arm's length while scoring his first international hat-trick.

He needed to after the first one, as Crichton did get his try in the second half after Walsh dropped a bomb.

Magic and mistakes go hand in hand, which is the risk Walters has taken by preferring Walsh at full-back to James Tedesco - who was player of the match as he helped Sydney Roosters win last month's NRL Grand Final.

"That's Reece," Walters repeated when asked about the errors. "He brings great stuff to the team.

"His catching of the high ball, it's difficult and sometimes you don't get a hold of them. He didn't tonight but it's not really anything we've got too much concern with."

Walsh-inspired Australia crush irate Samoa to reach World Cup final

Australia reach World Cup final after Fiji scare

Victory maintains Australia's 100% record at this tournament, with 170 points scored across four matches.

Their last defeat at a World Cup was against New Zealand in the 2008 final. They have won 22 consecutive games since then, winning the past three tournaments.

To avoid a repeat of 2008 when the meet the Kiwis in Brisbane next Sunday, they will need Walsh at his best to deal with the returned Kalyn Ponga.

New Zealand full-back Ponga, who battled on for 20 minutes with a broken arm in their thrilling 24-22 opening game defeat by Australia, remarkably returned for the semi-final against Tonga on Saturday and produced a man-of-the-match display.

In that opener back on 15 October, Walsh delivered a superb try-saving tackle on opposite number Ponga during the first half before scoring with a sensational 60-metre burst to lay the platform for the Kangaroos' last-gasp victory.

That was despite the fact that, in the run-up to the World Cup, Walsh had not played for eight weeks because of an ankle injury.

Afterwards he was vomiting in the changing room because of the effort, according to Walters. He may need to plunge those depths again.

"We all know Kalyn," said Walters. "He's a world-class player; he showed that last night.

"For the players, it's been about what we can do as a team. If we get that right, I'm happy with that."

'You guys saw the game. You report on it.'

For Samoa, a second successive World Cup ends in defeat by Australia, after being beaten 30-10 in the final four years ago.

The two nations have met six times, with Australia winning all six.

But this one hurt more. Samoa clearly felt they could win, as their ultra-aggressive Siva Tau war dance pre-match proved – getting right in the Australian faces, even forehead to forehead in some cases.

But they were aggrieved by some debatable refereeing decisions, including two disallowed tries – Crichton in the first half, then Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow denied with 10 minutes to go after contact between Manuleleua and Liam Martin was deemed illegal.

It bubbled over shortly before the break, when Spencer Leniu was sin-binned for dissent by Australian referee Adam Gee.

"You guys saw the game. You report on it," was Samoa coach Ben Gardiner's terse response to questions about the decisions.

On whether his side cost themselves with a lack of discipline, he said: "I'm not quite sure.

"On the back of some of the penalties that were given, we just didn't react very well. There was one thing into another and then a try. It made it difficult to be able to fight back from that.

"And then to be down by 18 points, 20 points at half-time, to chase back from that... I thought we did well in the second half to fight back.

"But then again, we scored a try and gave up another one straight away. We bounced off too many tackles in that early period, missed too many tackles in the game in general.

"That had nothing to do with the emotion. That's a Test match, that's what you do. It's physical, there's push and shove, stand your ground."

articles.title: England 45-22 Australia: Hosts swat aside Wallabies at Twickenham
articles.summary: England provide emphatic on-pitch backing for head coach Steve Borthwick as they swat aside a listless Australia at Allianz Stadium.
articles.body:
Tries: George, Chessum, Heyes, Van Poortvliet, Pollock (2), Spencer Cons: F Smith (5 )

Tries: Jorgensen, Daugunu, Williams Cons: Lonergan, Donaldson Pens: Lonergan

England provided emphatic on-pitch backing for head coach Steve Borthwick as they scored seven tries to swat aside a listless Australia at Allianz Stadium.

The build-up was marked by questions over England's form, which has been poor for most of 2026, and a reported rift between players and coaches during the summer.

Senior players angrily insisted on Friday the squad and staff were still united, and their performance on Sunday would demonstrate as such.

There are stiffer Tests to come, with New Zealand arriving in a fortnight, but Borthwick sailed through this referendum with flying colours.

His team played with determination and physicality, but also dexterity and ambition, in their most complete display of the year by a long margin.

They were heartily endorsed by the home crowd, who spent the final quarter serenading their side with Swing Low and willing Henry Pollock, brought on to fill in for wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, to complete a hat-trick after an enterprising cameo out wide.

Pollock was denied his third, but it was one of the few things his side missed out on during a most satisfying outing.

Feyi-Waboso brings X-factor before injury strikes again

Borthwick had made a fast start, along with tidying up discipline, a key aim for his side.

They seemed to have delivered on the former inside 120 seconds. After a typically bustling carry from Ben Earl, soft hands from the excellent Seb Atkinson and Fin Smith released Feyi-Waboso on a carving line that took him under the posts.

It was a moment full of the intensity, intention and invention that England are desperate to show.

Unfortunately for the hosts the celebrations were curtailed, with the score chalked off for Ben Curry's pass straying forward to Ollie Chessum in a previous phase.

On eight minutes, Australia's own indiscipline paved the way to the first England try.

After an obstruction as England chased a kick, Smith put his forwards into the corner and their driven maul survived Australia's counter and wound its way over the line, with Jamie George locked on for the score.

A loose and limp Australia provided the perfect backdrop for a statement in the first half.

Feyi-Waboso was the swerving, centre point of England's early endeavour.

After missing the entirety of the Six Nations through injury, the 23-year-old brings electric pace and evasion to the backline.

His break set up a prime position, deep inside Australia's 22m, for England's second try, with Henry Slade and George Furbank's raking miss passes giving Chessum room to canter in.

With Australia prop Angus Bell yellow-carded for a hip-drop tackle on Feyi-Waboso, Joe Heyes splintered off the side of a driven maul to put England 19-3 clear after little more than half an hour.

It was the least their dominance deserved.

However Max Jorgensen's interception on the stroke of half-time, picking off Jack van Poortvliet's pass to race away under the posts, evoked memories of 2024.

In the teams' meeting that year, Australia hung on to the coat-tails of a fast-starting England before Jorgensen scored a last-gasp decisive try to seal the Wallabies' win.

With Feyi-Waboso failing to return after the break, back row Pollock brought off the bench to fill a wing spot in the absence of back-three replacements and their lead only nine, England were not clear of danger.

However a delicious try, created by Furbank's pinpoint incision and deft offload, Freeman's inside pass and scorer Van Poortvliet's support line, restored England's cushion after the restart, in the final play before Bell's return from the sin bin.

A quick-fire double from Pollock extended the hosts' advantage. For his first try he snaffled a loose ball and picked a path to the line, before showing his pace from further out to round off a lovely move featuring Smith, Freeman and Furbank.

Australia were 38-10 down and set to record a losing margin against England, eclipsing the 24 points they were beaten by in 2017 and 2019.

Tries from Filipo Daugunu and Jeremy Williams in the final 20 minutes averted that fate, but there was no disguising the gulf between the teams.

With a home Rugby World Cup to come in less than a year, Wallabies boss Les Kiss, who was visibly angry in the coaches' box, has plenty of work to do.

So does Borthwick, who saw Ben Spencer intercept and dive over for his first Test try to round off victory.

He will have concerns over centre Atkinson, who departed with a painful-looking leg injury in the second half, and Feyi-Waboso, who emerged at full-time in a protective boot.

But the England head coach can advance into autumn in a position of considerably more comfort.

articles.title: Steve Borthwick and Maro Itoje reject reports of friction between England head coach and players after Australia win
articles.summary: Steve Borthwick to media on Sunday: "It's not an environment I recognise [newspaper article]. It's not an accurate reflection"; Maro Itoje: "That's not the man I recognise. The article doesn't represent the environment I recognise. If you speak to players, they will say a different story"
articles.body:
Speaking to media following Sunday's dominant 45-22 Nations Championship victory over Australia at Allianz Stadium Twickenham, Borthwick addressed the article for the first time since its publication on Friday.

Within it, The Times reported that some England players lost faith in Borthwick during a summer campaign which included a 45-21 defeat to world champions South Africa and a nervy win over Argentina.

It is alleged players objected to Borthwick's treatment of them, that he was involved in a training ground bust-up with Ellis Genge and that they wanted RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney - who this week unequivocally backed the head coach - to listen to their gripes.

Speaking to Sky Sports on Friday, Jamie George said England's players were "hurt" by the report , calling the timing of the article "shocking."

On Sunday, Borthwick said: "It's not an environment I recognise. It's not an accurate reflection.

"What I will say is that in the last couple of days, a number of my predecessors have reached out and contacted me, and they certainly did.

"They're always supportive, and I won't name who they are, but a number of them reached out to me and the basic gist of it is: 'Been there, got the t-shirt, focus on the rugby', and that's it.

"As England head coach you get that t-shirt, and what you do is focus on the rugby and that's what I've done this week, that's what the players have done, that's what every member of the staff around the players has done.

Itoje: We have full support in Borthwick

Sat next to Borthwick at Sunday's post-match press conference, England skipper Itoje gave a passionate defence of his head coach.

"From a player's point of view, we have full support in Steve," he said.

"I've had the privilege of Steve being my coach since 2016, with a little gap when he was in his Leicester years. That's not the man I recognise. The article doesn't represent the environment I recognise, and I think if you speak to players over his coaching career they will say a different story.

"Particularly, often you think about players from other countries. If you speak to some of those guys from the 2017 Lions tour [to New Zealand], they'll tell you about the impact Steve had on them.

"Those guys aren't English I'm talking about, I'm talking about the Irish guys, I'm talking about the Welsh guys who he had the pleasure of coaching and having an influence on.

"Just from a player's point of view, as always there's things that we want to get right, there's things that we try and put on the field, sometimes for whatever reason it doesn't quite click. I think often too much criticism is attached to the coach.

"Whereas, no matter how well Steve coaches us, we as players are the ones on the field. We as players are the ones who have to perform and put it right.

"There's been times where we haven't quite done that which has put a bit of pressure on him. I'm delighted that today we were able to get the win. He's a world-class coach and we're lucky to have him."

For England, they next face Japan in their second Nations Championship Test of the autumn at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Saturday November 14 (4.40pm kick-off).

articles.title: England 45-22 Australia: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso burns bright in win
articles.summary: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso's blistering first half display provides England fans with a glimpse of what could be in a much-needed statement of faith in coach Steve Borthwick.
articles.body:
That's what Bongi Mbonambi described it as.

After scraping past Steve Borthwick's side in the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final, the South Africa hooker was scathing of England's back-slapping and celebrating of in-game wins.

By then, it had already become something of a meme. Back row Ben Earl pumping his fist to celebrate Ireland's crooked line-out throw in a pre-tournament warm-up was a particular source of online mockery.

But, while it isn't the diesel grunt that can win matches on its own, "plastic energy" is still something.

It is the body language that shows mindset and intent, that a team's pilot light is on and burning bright.

England had it under Borthwick at the Stade de France three years ago, coming agonisingly close to derailing the Springboks. And they had it in spades in Sunday's 45-22 win against the Wallabies.

Earl, inevitably, was one outlet, loudly celebrating a third-minute scrum success.

But there were plenty more examples throughout the match. Jamie George bellowing into the stands after the opening score; captain Maro Itoje being surrounded with congratulations after an early charge-down; Henry Slade being embraced after a lung-busting late try-saving tackle on Max Jorgensen.

A report in the Times newspaper earlier in the week had said that a rift between the players and their coach opened in Argentina in July, at the end of the summer's campaign.

England's senior players denied it. Nothing more to see, they said, than the transparent honesty of a team where input is valued and improvement is the lodestar.

But, they also promised proof on the pitch against Australia. It was a risky gambit.

Another misfiring, disjointed, underpowered performance – like that in their most-recent visit to Twickenham, February's 42-21 defeat by Ireland - would dial up the pressure on Borthwick another notch.

Instead, his fired-up players turned up.

They did so in the obvious ways. There was gainline physicality, breakdown bravery and crunching physicality.

Ben Curry leaping out of the line to land a big hit on fly-half Declan Meredith was satisfyingly old school.

But there was more than that. There was a different sort of bravery – the one that dares to chance the arm, throw a final pass and back ability, rather than take a safe option.

Full-back George Furbank summed it up. Playing his first Test in nearly two years, his ball-playing smarts were deliciously demonstrated in Jack van Poortvliet's try, hitting a line, flashing a dummy and smuggling an offload to cut the Wallabies to ribbons.

Henry Slade and Seb Atkinson pulled strings expertly as well.

Immanuel Feyi-Waboso showed the sort of Test match mojo that England must protect at all costs.

The Exeter wing, who, like Furbank, has endured a rotten injury run, was electric in the first half.

Every time the 23-year-old touched the ball, expectation crackled around the stands. And it was mostly met.

In 40 minutes of rugby, Feyi-Waboso made 113m from eight carries, beating seven defenders.

All those figures were unmatched by any other England player despite the fact that Feyi-Waboso came off at the break and only played 32 minutes uninjured.

The wing's ankle was caught under prop Angus Bell's considerable heft and was cossetted in a protective boot as he watched the remainder of the match from the sidelines.

After Feyi-Waboso's absence from the entirety of England's Six Nations campaign, the decision not to remove him immediately and minimise the damage may be one they regret when the prognosis lands.

England looked to his pace, power and unpredictability as much as they could, feeding him on a dart off the blindside wing from one promising line-out position.

They may be missing it next week against Japan. And potentially beyond.

Henry Pollock, with a shock of freshly-peroxided hair, came on and inevitably stole the spotlight, with two tries in a cameo on the wing.

But, on the wing, Pollock is a stop-gap, while Feyi-Waboso is the star.

His fitness, along with that of Seb Atkinson, will be chief of Borthwick's concerns.

A cleaned-up disciplinary display – with seven penalties conceded and only the second time this year they have managed to avoid being shown a card – and breakdown that was quick and clean were major plus points.

The bench maintained their dominance with an all-Lions front row of Ellis Genge, Luke Cowan-Dickie and Will Stuart trotting on to turn the screw was a welcome sight.

"I am really proud," Borthwick told BBC Sport.

"These players are a wonderful group. We have had some bumps in the road. We have this age bubble where we have so many players 25 and under who are developing quickly into great Test match players, and we have an older group who are helping to guide them.

"It is an interesting balance and they are working so well together. They are a pleasure to work with."

Australia were desperately poor. Their players are in the midst of a pay dispute with Rugby Australia, an unwelcome distraction that has gone under the radar given the focus on Borthwick.

New Zealand, rejuvenated under new coach Dave Rennie, will offer a far more formidable stress test in a fortnight.

But as the team's energy spread to the stands, with the vast majority of the 81,334 won over by the display, Sunday was a victory for England to savour at the end of a difficult week.

articles.title: Louis Rees-Zammit: Wales wing in confident mood ahead of All Blacks
articles.summary: Wing Louis Rees-Zammit feels confident and looks sharp ahead of Wales' Nations Championship meeting with New Zealand.
articles.body:
Wales wing Louis Rees-Zammit says he has rediscovered his swagger as he aims to fight fire with fire against the All Blacks.

Rees-Zammit will be to the fore when Steve Tandy's side attempt to upset the odds against New Zealand in the Nations Championship on Saturday (14:10 GMT).

Wales go into the game after labouring to a 28-21 bonus-point victory against Japan at Principality Stadium.

It was an unconvincing performance, but Rees-Zammit stood out, scoring a try, making 12 carries for 121 metres and beating 13 defenders to be named man of the match.

He made more line breaks against Japan than he did in the entire Six Nations, when he started every game at full-back.

"I felt really confident out there and that's from the work in the week and at Bristol," said Rees-Zammit.

"I have found some confidence in my game and playing back on the wing helps. I feel I can create chances, help the team go forward and finish tries off."

Why Wales have a lot to prove despite beating Japan

Wales let themselves down despite win - Lake

Rees-Zammit is in his second season since returning to rugby from two years trying to make it in the NFL.

The 2021 British and Irish Lions tourist has crossed five times in five games for Bristol and is second in the Prem for defenders beaten (28), fifth for metres gained (299) and third for clean breaks (12).

He said: "I am just playing with a smile on my face, playing with confidence and always thinking that I can beat defenders, and in defence I feel really good as well."

Rees-Zammit assessment is backed up by Wales' record try scorer.

Shane Williams told the Scrum V podcast: "He's a confident young man isn't he? He's definitely looking bigger and sharper than he has for some time.

"I know he's been talking about that he's put a bit of weight on and he's stronger and faster, but the proof's in the pudding.

Williams, who scored 60 tries in 91 Test appearances for Wales and the British and irish Lions, was impressed by Rees-Zammit's performance in the opening autumn fixture.

"He certainly looked the business against Japan. It's encouraging to see him get involved in the game nice and early taking defenders on.

"He looked sharp. Whether he's going to be able to bump off the All Blacks defenders the way he did on on Saturday, I'm not sure.

"But it's encouraging, he took his try well and was busy throughout."

Tandy's side now host a New Zealand side that impressively stretched away from Scotland in the second half in a comprehensive 43-21 success.

Wales have lost 34 straight games to the All Blacks since their 1953 triumph, a streak that few expect to end in Cardiff.

But Rees-Zammit takes encouragement from last November's meeting when New Zealand won 52-26 - but led just 24-21 early in the second half.

"Last year we were in it until 60-odd minutes. It's about hard work and putting your body on the line against those boys," said the wing, who scored an acrobatic try against New Zealand last year.

"Then when you get the ball and get chances, be brave with it, be fearless because we have a strong back line and players who can finish.

"Next week will be brave and go for it. They are obviously a great team, but the second that you shy away from it, you miss and they take advantage."

After left wing Tom Rogers became the first Welsh player to score a hat-trick against New Zealand last year, Rees-Zammit will hope for plenty of chances to show his finishing prowess on the right flank next weekend.
