articles.title: Nations Championship: England's unique Henry Pollock, impressive pack performance, concerning injuries, remaining issues after win vs Australia
articles.summary: Steve Borthwick's side got their autumn Nations Championship campaign off to flying start with record points win vs Australia at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham; Unique Henry Pollock shows impressive versatility on wing; England's pack impress with brains and brawn; Worrying backline injuries
articles.body:
Unique Pollock shows impressive versatility on the wing

One of the main concerns for a head coach when selecting a 6-2 replacements bench, as opposed to a more conventional 5-3 split of forwards to backs, is backline injuries.

Owing to the fact one of the two backs in a 6-2 must be a scrum-half, that leaves just one player covering fly-half, centre, wings and full-back, or able to cover some of those positions with a rejig of other players on the pitch.

What is unique in rugby at the moment is the presence of a small pool of genuine hybrid players. That is to say, players who can perform as a forward and as a back.

Levani Botia for Fiji and Andre Esterhuizen for South Africa are two such examples of players who have played at back-row and centre. France's Oscar Jegou came on as a centre in Dublin in 2025 and performed superbly despite being a back-row, while England back-row Ben Earl was been touted as a potential centre option.

On Sunday against Australia, England had a bench with scrum-half Ben Spencer and Marcus Smith - who can play at fly-half and full-back - as recognised backs.

Wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso - sensational during the first half - suffered an ankle injury and limped through to half-time, and when it became clear he could not continue, back-row Henry Pollock was the man chosen to come onto the wing.

At that point in the match, the difference was only nine points in favour of England - hardly a Test wrapped up - but Pollock's very first carry on the wing was fantastic, motoring and fighting forward for some 10 metres to get into the Australia half.

In fact, it set in motion England's attack which eventually saw Tommy Freeman race on down the right and pass inside for Jack van Poortvliet to score the bonus-point clinching fourth try. The hosts never looked back from there.

Better was to follow from the 21-year-old Pollock: two superb finishes on the opposite flank as part of slick backline moves run by fly-half Fin Smith where Pollock scored twice in two minutes to wrap up the match as a contest.

There's a lot of noise from and around him, but all-action back-row with superb breakdown skills and the pace of a back? Well add part-time winger to Pollock's resume now too. And that is a huge asset for Steve Borthwick and England. Potentially priceless, even.

England's pack impress with brains and brawn

While England's backline moved the ball superbly on Sunday afternoon, their attacks were only possible thanks to their pack, who built platforms around the field for their backs to launch attacks from.

Jamie George led the forwards superbly and crossed over for England's first try, with the hosts showing not only their devastating power, but how smart they can be with their mauling game when they get close to the line.

After winning a lineout five metres from the tryline, with Ollie Chessum delivering brilliant service off the top all game, Australia disrupted England's first maul. George, taking possession at the back, spotted a weak link in Australia's defence and cutely peeled off with a group of his team-mates, before bulldozing over the tryline.

A similar story unfolded for England's third try, with the hosts opting to maul again, before tighthead Joe Heyes spotted a gap on the fringes and skirted over.

Both tries were a brilliant combination of brains and brawn.

At the scrum, Heyes got an early victory over Angus Bell, forcing the Australian prop to stand up and concede a penalty. But at times, England were complacent, conceding a couple of silly free kicks for early engagements in vital field positions.

Lapses in concentration is one area England must improve on, with the hosts giving away silly penalties at the breakdown at critical moments. Alex Coles carelessly went off his feet while entering a ruck in the first-half, just as England were beginning to build momentum, with England conceding a penalty as a result.

Despite that, England were impressive with their rucking game and power through the contact. They outclassed Australia for physicality, which is no mean feat, given the strength of the Wallabies' pack.

For all that the final scoreline at Twickenham on Sunday made for impressive reading, and England's players and coaching staff will rightly be contented, there remain issues which cannot get lost.

The amount of errors in the first half alone could, and would, prove so costly for England against better sides.

Indeed, cough up that amount of 22 entries against South Africa, New Zealand, France and Ireland, and the chance of victory would be slim to none.

George Furbank was penalised for a neck roll, Coles was pinged for going off feet, Feyi-Waboso spilled possession on the run, Heyes was pinged for an early shove at an England scrum, George had a lineout throw ruled crooked, a scrum penalty was conceded, and Furbank also knocked on a grubber-kick - all of which occurred in the Australia 22 in the first half.

Each were pressure-relieving moments, and when Van Poortvliet's telegraphed pass was then picked off for a Max Jorgensen intercept try in the final minute of the half, the England lead was nine points when they could have been out of sight.

At present, England remain too profligate and it feels too easy for sides to get back into contests against them.

Borthwick's charges also struggled to get on the right side of referee Pierre Brousset at the scrum, finishing with just a 78 per cent success rate despite possessing a pack that monstered Australia for most of the match. That has to be sorted.

They also conceded 11 turnovers in the Test, but it wasn't costly as they won 17. Australia produced a horror-show of a display, but it's clear England impressed in several areas too.

So overall, a good day? Yes. But there remains plenty of work to do.

With big games coming up against New Zealand and Japan, Borthwick will be sweating on the fitness of both Feyi-Waboso and Seb Atkinson, who both came off injured on Sunday.

Seven minutes from half-time, Feyi-Waboso limped to the touchline in some pain after appearing to twist his right leg in a hip-drop tackle by Angus Bell, who was handed a yellow card.

Feyi-Waboso was replaced at half-time by Pollock, and after the match, was seen wearing a support boot as he walked onto the field to celebrate with his team-mates.

Borthwick confirmed his injury needed to be assessed, a concerning update given the Exeter winger is one of England's most exciting outlets and caused headaches for Australia's defence throughout.

Atkinson hobbled off in the 65th minute after appearing to suffer a hip injury.

Thankfully for the England centre, Borthwick confirmed his injury was not too serious.

For England, they next face Japan in their second Nations Championship Test of the autumn at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Saturday November 14 (4.40pm kick-off).

articles.title: Nations Championship: Matt Dawson column - England make massive step up in 45-22 win vs Australia
articles.summary: In his latest column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on an impressive win for Steve Borthwick's side against Australia in the Nations Championship.
articles.body:
In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on an impressive 45-22 win for Steve Borthwick's side against Australia in the Nations Championship on Sunday.

Beating Australia with their record points tally against the Wallabies was a very positive way for England to start the autumn series, given the break they have had and how the beginning of the year went.

England were very accurate, very disciplined, creative and genuinely did not give Australia a sniff.

Before the game, I was expecting Australia to provide much more of a stern test. Some people might be a bit too critical of Australia, saying they did not turn up, but I think it edges more towards how well England played than how average Australia were.

I am not saying by any stretch that it was the perfect performance but, all in all, it was a massive step up from the Six Nations and even from the Nations Championship games in the summer.

Intensity, accuracy and discipline in abundance

A couple of days before the Australia game, Jamie George said the England team had been galvanised by a newspaper article which claimed the end of their summer tour had been marked by player unrest over head coach Borthwick's leadership.

When you are inside those international camps, you are very deliberate in staying tight and not letting anybody in in whatever way, shape or form, therefore you become very sensitive to any kind of criticism.

There is a reason for doing that - it draws you together and allows you to create a bit more determination and drive to be successful.

You could see England's intensity, their accuracy and their discipline. All the things that have maybe been highlighted over the past nine months as things England have been lacking, there was an abundance of all of it.

As much as it is easy to try to pick holes in England because it is England, sometimes you have got to pat people on the back and say they got it right.

The opposition was dangerous with good individual players, but from the off England's tactics were spot on. Their decision-making was controlled and they looked like a very well-drilled side.

England swat aside Wallabies to back up Borthwick

Feyi-Waboso burns bright as England energy endorses Borthwick

How England might unlock the best of Slade

England's back three of George Furbank, Tommy Freeman and Immanuel Feyi-Waboso caused plenty of problems for Australia, but I think you have to include Fin Smith and Henry Slade in that as well.

Potentially, there is something in that backline that may allow us to see the Slade we see for Exeter that we have not seen as much for England.

Having the likes of Feyi-Waboso, Freeman and Furbank around Slade and them understanding the sorts of positions he can get them into - there might be some long-term benefits to that.

Feyi-Waboso is X-factor, there is no question about that. For his early disallowed try, he shifted his weight and beat someone with that pace - I do not think there are many people in the world who could do that.

When you have got players like him who can do that regularly, all of a sudden you are getting momentum.

There was a massive difference in ruck speed and in momentum; England were getting lined up defensively and pushing Australia back, whereas when you have got players like Feyi-Waboso and Ben Earl, and then when Henry Pollock comes on as well, you have got plenty of players who can break the line in traffic and it makes attacking that much easier.

Fin Smith is leading the team, he looks like he is a general and in control of the game.

He has got a safe pair of hands and communication from Seb Atkinson, he has got vision from Slade and then a back three that if you give them half a chance, they are going to bust the line, create opportunities and probably finish.

There were bits of Sunday's game where if New Zealand were doing it, everybody would be ranting and raving about how complete some of those tries were.

Pollock's flexibility a fantastic weapon

Feyi-Waboso's injury meant Pollock came off the bench to play in an unfamiliar position on the wing and he ended up scoring two of England's seven tries.

He did very well considering he was on for a whole half. Going forward, what is the difference having Pollock there? He has got a winger's speed, the step, great hands, the power and the bulk that other wingers do not have and he is going to be a handful for the opposition.

Defensively, he was tested a couple of times and that is inevitable, but to have that flexibility on the bench allows England to have that six-two split because you have got a player who can now pretty much cover so many positions.

As great as it was, and I am sure he absolutely loved it, unfortunately he is probably inking himself in to be quite a significant bench player moving forward, which is not really what I think he would like to be labelled as.

Selfishly, from an England point of view, it is a fantastic weapon to have.

The whole bench did really well and made a difference. It goes all the way back to selection, something Borthwick has previously come under fire for a little bit.

It does not mean that just because he has got one right, the autumn is going to go swimmingly well, but from the off the selection has been right, the gameplan was a bit more expansive than I thought it was going to be and they absolutely nailed the execution.

Tactically, I loved the balance of the England performance; a really dominant set-piece, driving mauls and in-your-face defence.

England have maybe always been like that but have lacked the discipline to go with it.

Against Australia, they proved they have the capability to be disciplined and maintain concentration - and I want to see that over the next three weeks.

Can they, under more pressure - because they are going to face more pressure, particularly against New Zealand - still maintain that discipline and decision-making?

They have got the assets to overpower Japan, but can they do it by giving away fewer than 10 penalties? Can they do it by having 15 people on the pitch for 80 minutes?

All of the little things they have been after, can they do them against a team they should beat comfortably?

If they can, then when they go into the New Zealand game with it all to play for and when they are really testing themselves, they are going to have huge momentum.

Matt Dawson was speaking to BBC Sport's Phil Cartwright.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: 2030 edition to be in USA and Pacific Islands
articles.summary: The 2030 Rugby League World Cup tournament will be hosted by the USA and the Pacific Islands, but the five host cities are yet to be confirmed.
articles.body:
The 2030 edition of the Rugby League World Cup will be held in the USA and the Pacific Islands.

The five host cities are yet to be confirmed, but the men's and women's tournaments will run concurrently, as they are with this year's ongoing tournament which is being held in Australia.

World governing body International Rugby League (IRL) said the aim was to expand the sport's reach to new countries.

"This is a strategy to maximise the interest of broadcasters, government partners and fans in the current World Cup, which has regularly broken records for crowds and the number of television viewers," IRL chairman Tony Grant said at the board's annual general meeting (AGM) in Sydney.

"At the same time we want to take advantage of opportunities that are opening up in new frontiers where the Rugby League World Cup hasn't previously been played."

Grant also confirmed that the men's World Cup would expand from 10 teams to 12, while the women's event would consist of 10 instead of eight.

The format of the tournament is yet to be decided after nations were asked for their feedback at the AGM, while the IRL has also proposed that Samoa and Tonga be promoted to Tier One nations alongside Australia, England and New Zealand.

Samoa became the first Pacific country to play in a World Cup final in 2022, while they and Tonga both reached the semi-finals of this year's tournament.

The 2030 Wheelchair World Cup will take place at the same time, but will be held in France, while the 2034 tournament will be hosted in Europe.

Both men's and women's finals of the 2026 tournament are being contested between Australia and New Zealand, in Brisbane on Sunday 15 November.

Australia's men have won the past three World Cups while their women are playing in their fifth successive final.
